lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Phrasal verbs: meanings, object placement and gap-fill choices
objectives: Explain what a phrasal verb is and give the meaning of eight common single-particle phrasal verbs (turn down, give in, run across, call off, turn up, put off, come across, come through) with new example sentences.
State the meanings of eight further phrasal verbs (hook up, give up, round off, round up, turn out, break into, touch down, cut in) and use them in correct sentences.
Choose the correct phrasal verb in gap-fill sentences, including get through to, come off, turn out, make away with and look up to, using meaning and grammar, and place a pronoun object correctly.
lessons.body:
A phrasal verb is a verb followed by one or two small words, called particles (up, down, off, out, in, across, to), that together carry one meaning. The meaning is usually not the sum of the parts: in “The team refused to give in”, give in means surrender, not give something inside. Compare a literal use, “She ran across the road” (she crossed it), with a phrasal use, “She ran across an old friend” (she met him by chance). Many phrasal verbs have more than one meaning, so the sentence around the verb decides which meaning is intended.
Eight common phrasal verbs, each with a meaning and an example. Turn down means refuse or reject: “The bank turned down her request for a loan.” Give in means stop resisting and yield: “After a long argument the committee gave in and changed the date.” Run across means meet or find by chance: “I ran across my old exercise book while tidying the shelf.” Call off means cancel: “The match was called off because the pitch was flooded.” Turn up means arrive or appear: “Only ten students turned up for the extra lesson.” Put off means postpone: “We put off the trip until the roads were repaired.” Come across means meet or find by chance, and with as it means give a certain impression: “We came across a rare book in the market”; “She comes across as very confident.” Come through means survive a difficulty and reach the end of it safely, or do what was promised: “The village came through the flood without losing a single life”; “The promised funds finally came through.”
Do not reduce come through to the single word experience. Someone who has come through hardship has been through it and is still standing, so the idea of surviving is part of the meaning. A one-word gloss can drop part of a phrasal verb's meaning, so check a dictionary entry before relying on it.
Where the object goes. Some phrasal verbs take an object, and with many of them the object may sit between the verb and the particle: “They called off the match” or “They called the match off”. When the object is a pronoun it must go in the middle: “They called it off”, not “They called off it”. Turn down and put off behave in the same way. Run across and come across keep the particle beside the verb, so a pronoun follows them: “We ran across him.” Give in and turn up take no object.
Eight more phrasal verbs, with their usual meanings. Hook up means connect equipment to a power supply, a network or another device: “The technician hooked up the printer to the computer.” Give up means stop trying, or stop doing something regularly: “He gave up smoking last year.” Round off means finish something in a satisfying way, or change a number to a convenient nearby value: “We rounded off the programme with a song”; “Round 4.67 off to 4.7.” Round up means gather people or animals together, or raise a number to the next whole figure: “The herdsman rounded up the goats before dark.” Turn out has several meanings. It can mean prove to be in the end: “The rumour turned out to be false.” It can mean attend or gather in numbers: “A large crowd turned out to welcome the team.” It can also mean produce: “The bakery turns out two hundred loaves a day.” Break into means enter a place by force, usually to steal, and also begin something suddenly: “Thieves broke into the shop at night”; “The children broke into song.” Touch down means, of an aircraft, land: “The plane touched down in Lagos at noon.” Cut in means interrupt someone who is speaking, or move into the path of a vehicle in front of you: “She cut in with a question before he had finished.”
A four-step method for gap-fill questions about phrasal verbs. First, read the whole sentence and say in your own words what the gap must mean. Second, choose the option whose whole phrase has that meaning, not the one with a familiar first word: options often share a verb (come along, come off, come on, come up), so the particle is the whole question. Third, check the grammar: does the sentence need an object, or a word such as to or with after the phrase? Fourth, read the sentence again with your choice in place.
Worked example. “The fund-raising plan ___ better than anyone expected.” The gap means succeeded or worked out. Come off can mean succeed or happen as planned; come up means arise; come along means accompany or make progress; come on means hurry or improve. Come off fits: “The fund-raising plan came off better than anyone expected.”
Some phrasal verbs need a word after them, and that word cannot be dropped. Get through to means succeed in reaching someone, usually by telephone: “After six attempts I got through to the manager.” Make away with means steal something and escape with it: “The burglar made away with the radio.” Look up to means admire and respect: “Pupils look up to a teacher who is fair.” The words to and with belong to the phrase, not to the noun that follows.
When a question asks you to use a phrasal verb in a sentence, let the other words show the meaning: “We put off the meeting until Friday” shows postponement because of until Friday. Keep the verb in the right form for the sentence: turned down, turns down, is turning down.

practice.question: In your own words, say what a phrasal verb is. Then explain how ran across differs in “She ran across the road” and “She ran across an old friend”.
practice.answer: A phrasal verb is a verb combined with a particle (or two) so that the whole phrase has one meaning that cannot be worked out from the separate words. In “She ran across the road” the verb is literal: she crossed the road by running. In “She ran across an old friend” ran across is a phrasal verb meaning met by chance.

marking.criterion: a verb combined with a particle or particles
the whole phrase has one meaning that is not the sum of its parts
first sentence literal: crossed the road by running
second sentence phrasal: met or found by chance

practice.question: Complete each sentence with the correct form of one of these phrasal verbs: call off, turn down, give in, run across, turn up, put off, come across, come through. (1) The organisers have ___ the concert because the hall is flooded. (2) Ada ___ the job offer because the pay was too low. (3) After three days of pressure, the council finally ___ and lowered the fee. (4) While sorting the cupboard, Tunde ___ his father's old watch. (5) Fewer than twenty pupils ___ for the early lesson. (6) The coach ___ the match until Saturday because the pitch was wet. (7) In interviews she ___ as calm and confident. (8) The family ___ the earthquake with only minor damage.
practice.answer: (1) called off; (2) turned down; (3) gave in; (4) ran across (came across is also acceptable); (5) turned up; (6) put off, because the match is moved to a later day, not cancelled; (7) comes across, the only verb that can be followed by as in the sense of giving an impression; (8) came through.

practice.question: Write two sentences using turn out, each with a different meaning, and state the meaning of turn out in each.
practice.answer: Model answer: “The rumour turned out to be false.” (turn out = prove to be in the end). “Hundreds of voters turned out on Saturday.” (turn out = attend or gather in numbers). Producing goods is also acceptable as a third meaning if used correctly. Any two different, correct senses earn the marks.

marking.criterion: first sentence uses turn out correctly
second sentence uses turn out correctly in a different sense

practice.question: Give one meaning of each phrasal verb: hook up, give up, round off, round up, turn out, break into, touch down, cut in.
practice.answer: hook up: connect equipment to a power supply, network or device. give up: stop trying, or stop doing something regularly. round off: finish something in a satisfying way, or change a number to a convenient nearby value. round up: gather people or animals together, or raise a number to the next whole figure. turn out: prove to be, attend in numbers, or produce. break into: enter by force, or begin suddenly. touch down: of an aircraft, land. cut in: interrupt a speaker, or move into the path of a vehicle ahead. Any correct sense from the lesson earns the mark.

practice.question: Rewrite each sentence, replacing the noun phrase after the verb (the match, the offer, the manager) with a pronoun: (1) They called off the match. (2) She turned down the offer. (3) We ran across the manager.
practice.answer: (1) They called it off. (2) She turned it down. (3) We ran across him.

marking.criterion: (1) pronoun placed between call and off
(2) pronoun placed between turn and down

practice.question: Choose the best option and say in a few words why it fits. (1) After several failed attempts, she finally ___ to her cousin on the phone. (a) got at (b) got through (c) got over (d) got off. (2) Young players ___ the captain because of his honesty and skill. (a) look up to (b) look down on (c) look after (d) look into. (3) The surprise party ___ very well and everyone was delighted. (a) came off (b) came up (c) came along (d) came on. (4) Nearly all the villagers ___ to welcome the new chief. (a) turned over (b) turned out (c) turned down (d) turned away. (5) In the night a fox ___ with two of the chickens. (a) made up (b) made out (c) made away (d) made over.
practice.answer: (1) b, got through to means succeeded in reaching someone by phone. (2) a, look up to means admire and respect; look down on means despise. (3) a, came off means succeeded or happened as planned. (4) b, turned out means attended in numbers. (5) c, made away with means stole and escaped with. Each item scores one mark for the option and one for a correct reason.

practice.question: Write a short paragraph of three sentences about a school event. Use three different phrasal verbs from this lesson and list them after the paragraph.
practice.answer: Model answer: “The inter-house sports were put off because of rain. On Saturday a large crowd turned out to cheer. The head teacher rounded off the day with a short speech.” Any three different phrasal verbs used correctly in sense and form earn the marks.

marking.criterion: first sentence: phrasal verb used in a correct sense
first sentence: correct form and grammar
second sentence: phrasal verb used in a correct sense
second sentence: correct form and grammar
third sentence: phrasal verb used in a correct sense
third sentence: correct form and grammar

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Adverbs, conjunctions and prepositions: formation, function and dependent pairs
objectives: Form adverbs from adjectives with -ly and its spelling changes, recognise -wards and -wise adverbs, and identify adverbs that have no special ending, correcting the source list's 'if', repeated 'very' and indoor/outdoor entries.

Distinguish adjuncts, disjuncts and conjuncts and identify each in a sentence, recognising that at six o'clock is a prepositional phrase functioning as an adverbial and that alternatively differs from alternately.
Identify subordinating conjunctions and the subordinate clauses they introduce, and distinguish them from relative pronouns such as which, who and whose.
Supply the correct dependent preposition for common word-and-preposition pairs, including the corrected pairs indifferent to, spy on, die of or from, and hinge on.
Recognise and use phrase prepositions, including the corrected in view of and the completed in addition to, in complete sentences.
lessons.body:
This lesson brings together three word classes that the Week 2 scheme treats in one section: adverbs, conjunctions and prepositions. It reviews five lists whose wording needs correction, so every corrected point is taught here in fresh words rather than copied from the source. The original pages remain in the course unchanged; this lesson is a reviewed equivalent that learners can use beside them. The thread running through the lesson is the difference between what a word is (its class) and what it does in a sentence (its function), because several of the source errors come from confusing the two.
An adverb modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb, and sometimes it comments on a whole clause. Most adverbs of manner are built from an adjective by adding -ly: careful becomes carefully, quick becomes quickly, certain becomes certainly, and fortunate becomes fortunately. The spelling sometimes changes: happy becomes happily, gentle becomes gently, basic becomes basically, true becomes truly, and full becomes fully. A group of direction words ends in -wards: downwards, upwards, forwards, backwards, homewards and eastwards. British English often prefers -wards while American English often uses -ward; both forms are adverbs. A smaller group ends in -wise and expresses manner or viewpoint: clockwise, anticlockwise, lengthwise and crosswise, and, in informal speech, moneywise, foodwise and weather-wise. In formal writing, phrases such as with regard to money are safer than moneywise. Many common adverbs have no special ending at all: always, early, fast, hard, late, often, quite, soon, very and well. Learn these as words, not as adjectives waiting for a suffix. Notice that hard and hardly, late and lately, and near and nearly are different words with different meanings: to work hard means to work with effort, while to hardly work means almost not to work at all. Two corrections follow from this. First, indoor and outdoor are adjectives; the adverbs are indoors and outdoors, formed with -s and not with -ly, so they do not belong in a list of -ly formations. Second, if is a conjunction, not an adverb, and very should appear only once in a list.
Adverbs and adverbial phrases do different jobs. An adjunct is an adverbial that belongs to the central message of the clause. It usually answers how, when, where, how often or to what extent: she answered calmly (how), we meet tomorrow (when), they waited outside (where), he visits often (how often), and the bag was almost empty (to what extent). An adjunct can be a single adverb, an adverb phrase or a prepositional phrase. This is why at six o'clock is a prepositional phrase working as an adverbial, not a single adverb word; the source example confuses the form of the phrase with the class of a word. When you are asked to identify an adjunct, name its function and the question it answers, then say what form carries it.
A disjunct comments on the whole statement rather than on how the action was done. It usually shows the speaker's attitude, judgement or view of the truth of the remark: fortunately, the bus arrived on time; frankly, I do not agree; undoubtedly, she is the best candidate; foolishly, he ignored the warning; and seriously, we need a plan. Disjuncts are often placed first and marked off by a comma, though they can also appear in the middle of a clause. Other common disjuncts are honestly, strangely, happily, fortunately, seriously and undoubtedly. Ask yourself whether the word tells you how something happened or what the speaker thinks about it; the second answer points to a disjunct.
A conjunct is a linking adverb. It shows the logical relation between two clauses or sentences: the road was flooded; nevertheless, we set out (concession); she is hard-working; besides, she is kind (addition); the price rose; consequently, sales fell (result); bring a pen; otherwise, you cannot write (alternative consequence); meanwhile, the others waited (time); and similarly, the second group improved (comparison). A conjunct can usually be moved or removed without breaking the grammar of its clause, which is one way to tell it apart from a conjunction. Use a semicolon or a full stop before a conjunct that links two statements, and a comma after it. One correction matters here: alternatively introduces a second possibility (we can travel by bus; alternatively, we can take the train), while alternately means in turn, one after the other (the lights flashed alternately). The source list uses alternately where the connective sense needs alternatively.
A conjunction joins words, phrases or clauses. There are three main kinds. Coordinating conjunctions are and, but, or, nor, for, so and yet; they join units of equal grammatical rank: bread and butter, slowly but surely, and we came but you were absent. Correlative conjunctions work in pairs: either...or, neither...nor, both...and, and not only...but also, as in both James and Jerry attended, and she is not only intelligent but also kind. Subordinating conjunctions introduce a subordinate clause: after, although, as, because, before, even though, if, in order that, since, so that, though, unless, until, when, whereas and while. Two corrections follow. First, which, who and whose are relative pronouns, not subordinating conjunctions: they stand for a noun and introduce a relative clause (the book which I bought; the pupil who won; the girl whose bag was lost). The word that can be either a relative pronoun or a subordinating conjunction, so decide from its work in the sentence. Second, say subordinate clause, not subordinating clause: the clause is subordinate, while the conjunction that introduces it is subordinating.
A subordinate clause cannot stand alone as a complete sentence, because the subordinating conjunction makes it depend on a main clause. It can come first or second. When it comes first, a comma usually separates it from the main clause: when the bell rang, the pupils left; although it was raining, the match continued; because the road was flooded, we stayed indoors. When it comes second, a comma is often unnecessary: the pupils left when the bell rang; the match continued although it was raining; we stayed indoors because the road was flooded. To test a clause, read it alone: when the bell rang does not make a complete statement, so it is subordinate. The conjunction is the word that signals the dependence.
A preposition shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and another word, often a relationship of place, time, direction, manner or cause. Simple prepositions include at, in, on, by, for, from, of, to, with, without, under, over, between and among. A dependent preposition is one whose choice is fixed by the word before it, so the pair must be learned together: allergic to, subjected to, stare at, convicted of, indicted for, victim of, charge with, abide by a rule, abide with a person, good at, bad at, quick at, kick against, connive at, frown at, consist of, confidence in, confide in, senior to, junior to, related to, agree to a plan, agree with a person, part with, recoil from, popular with, tremble with, differ with or from, comply with, blame something on someone, wait on or upon, and look forward to. Several source items need correction. The word is indifferent to, written as one word, not in different to. We spy on someone, not spy at someone. People die of or from an illness, not die on it. The dictionary form of the verb is hinge on, so we write the decision hinges on the evidence, using hinges as the third-person form. Arrive in is used with a city or country, and arrive at with a building or other point. Agree to takes a plan or proposal, while agree with takes a person. Look forward to ends with a preposition, so a verb after it takes -ing: we look forward to hearing from you. Use each pair in a full sentence, because the sentence is what shows whether the relationship is right.
A phrase preposition is a fixed group of words that does the work of one preposition. Common examples are in agreement with, in compliance with, in apposition with, because of, in view of, in accordance with, for the sake of, on account of, with regard to, with reference to, with respect to, in spite of, by reason of, in case of, in regard to, by means of, along with, in consideration of, contrary to, and in addition to. Two source items need correction. The phrase is in view of, without the article a. The final item in the source is cut off; the standard phrase is in addition to, as in in addition to the fee, learners pay for materials. These phrases are useful in formal writing because they express exact relationships: in spite of the rain, the event held; the policy was changed in accordance with the new law; by means of a map, the team found the site; with regard to your letter, we have no objection. Keep the whole phrase together and check that the noun after it fits the meaning.
When you meet these topics in a test, work in four steps. First, read the whole sentence and decide what job the target word or phrase is doing: modifying an action, commenting on the statement, linking two statements, joining units, or showing a relationship. Second, name the class and the function separately, because an adverb phrase can act as an adjunct and a prepositional phrase can do the same job. Third, for prepositions, find the word that controls the choice and recall the pair, not the preposition alone. Fourth, check punctuation and agreement: a conjunct between two statements needs a semicolon or full stop before it, a fronted subordinate clause usually needs a comma, and a singular subject such as the decision takes hinges, not hinge. A worked example: in fortunately, the team arrived before the rain started, fortunately is a disjunct commenting on the whole statement, before the rain started is a subordinate clause introduced by the subordinating conjunction before, and no adverb modifies arrived in this sentence. Read the sentence again after choosing, and let the meaning decide between look-alikes such as alternatively and alternately.

practice.question: Form an adverb from each adjective and write the whole word: (1) happy, (2) gentle, (3) basic, (4) true, (5) full, (6) quick, (7) careful, (8) certain.
practice.answer: (1) happily; (2) gently; (3) basically; (4) truly; (5) fully; (6) quickly; (7) carefully; (8) certainly.

practice.question: Say whether the word in capitals is an adjunct, a disjunct or a conjunct. (1) FORTUNATELY, the train was late. (2) She answered the question CALMLY. (3) The road was closed; NEVERTHELESS, we set out. (4) They waited OUTSIDE. (5) FRANKLY, I do not agree. (6) Bring a pen; OTHERWISE, you cannot write.
practice.answer: (1) disjunct; (2) adjunct; (3) conjunct; (4) adjunct; (5) disjunct; (6) conjunct.

practice.question: Choose the correct word. (1) We can walk; ___, we can take a bus. (alternatively / alternately) (2) The lights flashed ___. (alternatively / alternately) (3) The road was flooded; ___, we set out. (nevertheless / therefore) (4) She is kind; ___, she is patient. (besides / beside)
practice.answer: (1) alternatively; (2) alternately; (3) nevertheless, because the second statement contrasts with the first rather than following from it; (4) besides, because it adds a second quality. Beside is a preposition of place.

practice.question: For each sentence, write the subordinating conjunction and the subordinate clause. (1) When the bell rang, the pupils left. (2) We stayed indoors because the road was flooded. (3) Although it was raining, the match continued. (4) She will call you after she finishes.
practice.answer: (1) conjunction: when; subordinate clause: when the bell rang. (2) conjunction: because; subordinate clause: because the road was flooded. (3) conjunction: although; subordinate clause: although it was raining. (4) conjunction: after; subordinate clause: after she finishes.

marking.criterion: (1) subordinate clause when the bell rang
(2) subordinate clause because the road was flooded
(3) subordinate clause although it was raining

practice.question: Complete each sentence with the correct dependent preposition. (1) She is allergic ___ peanuts. (2) He is indifferent ___ praise. (3) The police spy ___ the suspect. (4) Many children die ___ malaria. (5) The decision hinges ___ the evidence. (6) He was convicted ___ theft. (7) I confide ___ my sister. (8) She is senior ___ me. (9) The teacher is popular ___ the pupils. (10) All staff must comply ___ the rules.
practice.answer: (1) to; (2) to; (3) on; (4) of (from is also acceptable); (5) on; (6) of; (7) in; (8) to; (9) with; (10) with.

practice.question: Rewrite each sentence correctly. (1) He is in different to criticism. (2) The guard spied at the visitor. (3) The old man died on fever. (4) The plan hinge in your support. (5) In a view of the rain, we stayed indoors. (6) In addition wit the fee, learners pay for materials.
practice.answer: (1) He is indifferent to criticism. (2) The guard spied on the visitor. (3) The old man died of fever (or died from fever). (4) The plan hinges on your support. (5) In view of the rain, we stayed indoors. (6) In addition to the fee, learners pay for materials.

practice.question: Complete each sentence with a phrase preposition from this list: in accordance with, because of, in spite of, with regard to, by means of, in addition to. (1) ___ the heavy rain, the match continued. (2) The rule was applied ___ the new policy. (3) ___ your letter, we have no objection. (4) The team found the site ___ a map. (5) ___ the fee, learners pay for materials. (6) The event was postponed ___ the flood.
practice.answer: (1) In spite of; (2) in accordance with; (3) With regard to; (4) by means of; (5) In addition to; (6) because of.

practice.question: Write five sentences about a school day. Use one adjunct, one disjunct, one conjunct, one subordinating conjunction and one phrase preposition. After each sentence, name the item you used.
practice.answer: Model answer: (1) The pupils assembled quietly in the hall. (adjunct: quietly) (2) Fortunately, the rain stopped before break. (disjunct: fortunately) (3) The library was closed; therefore, we studied in the classroom. (conjunct: therefore) (4) We finished the project because the teacher gave us extra time. (subordinating conjunction: because) (5) In spite of the noise, the class completed the test. (phrase preposition: in spite of) Any five sentences that use the five required items correctly and label them correctly earn the marks.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: The five essay types, the formal report and the minutes of a meeting
objectives: Distinguish the five essay types by purpose and name the organising features of each.
Plan a narrative essay as a sequence of stages, with one viewpoint and a consistent tense, and plan a descriptive essay around a dominant impression and ordered sensory detail.
Structure an expository essay using definition, process, cause and effect, or comparison and contrast.
Structure an argumentative essay with a disputable claim, supported reasons, a fair counterargument and a rebuttal, and recognise common fallacies.
Write a formal report to a named authority in the correct layout, using reported speech and consistent past tenses.
Record the minutes of a meeting in the correct order, with attendance, decisions, action points, adjournment and signatures.
lessons.body:
This lesson covers the Week 3 writing objectives: the five essay types named on the scheme of work, the formal report and the minutes of a meeting. The original page lists the five types and stops, and its report and minutes guidance breaks off early, so the teaching below is written here in fresh words and the source page stays unchanged. Every person, school and event used as an example is invented for practice. Start from purpose. A piece of writing is organised by what it has to do: recount, describe, explain, persuade, entertain, or report facts to someone in authority. Decide the purpose and the reader first, then choose the shape that serves them. All the forms in this lesson share a three-part frame—an opening that establishes the subject, a middle that develops it in paragraphs, and a close that finishes it—and all of them reward planning, drafting and editing in that order.
A narrative essay recounts a sequence of events so that the sequence makes a point. Its usual parts are the setting and the people involved, an opening situation, a complication that creates a difficulty, a climax where the difficulty comes to a head, a resolution, and a short reflection on what the experience showed. Keep one viewpoint throughout: either you take part (first person, I) or you tell it about someone else (third person, he, she, they). Keep the tense consistent: the past simple for the main events and the past perfect for anything that happened earlier. Signal the order with time links such as at first, meanwhile, by the time, after that and in the end, and cut anything that does not move the story. Show rather than tell: instead of saying that you were frightened, describe your hands shaking on the gate. A workable plan for “An incident that taught me patience” is: waiting in a queue with a friend; a quarrel about whose turn it is; an older person explains what happened; an apology; what I now do differently. The reflection belongs in the last lines, not in every paragraph.
A descriptive essay creates a clear impression of a person, a place, an object or an experience. Decide the dominant impression first—a market may be deafening, colourful or exhausting—and choose only details that build it. Use the senses in turn: sight, sound, smell, touch and, where it is natural, taste. Arrange the details in an order the reader can follow, usually spatial: from the gate to the courtyard, from the foreground to the background, or from the most striking feature to the least. Prefer precise nouns and strong verbs to piles of adjectives: instead of “a very big noisy crowd”, write “traders shouted prices over one another”. One simile or metaphor can carry an impression; used in every line it tires the reader. Keep the tense steady: the present for a scene you are observing as you write, the past for a remembered place. When the subject is a real person, describe what can be observed and do not invent private facts about them.
An expository essay explains or informs. It does not argue for a position; it makes a subject understood. Four patterns cover most school topics. Definition explains what something is and is not. Process explains how something is done, stage by stage, in time order. Cause and effect explains why something happened and what followed. Comparison and contrast explains a subject by setting it beside another, either point by point or subject by subject. Whichever pattern you use, state the subject and its main idea in the introduction, give one aspect per body paragraph with an example or detail, and close by drawing the parts together rather than introducing a new point. Use the present tense for general truths, as in “water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius”, and the past for a particular event. Keep the tone neutral, and define any term the reader may not know.
An argumentative essay defends a position. State the issue, then a claim that can reasonably be disputed: “boarding school is better than day school” is a claim, while “schools exist” is not. Support the claim with reasons, and support each reason with evidence—an example, a figure whose source you can name, or an accepted principle. Then take the strongest opposing view seriously, state it fairly, and answer it. That answer, the rebuttal, is what separates argument from assertion. In a short essay allow one paragraph for reasons and one for the counterargument and rebuttal; in a longer one, one paragraph per reason. Qualify where honesty requires it: should, is likely to and in most cases are stronger than always and never, because a single counter-example destroys an absolute claim. Avoid the common fallacies: generalising from one case, assuming that because two things happened together one caused the other, attacking the person instead of the argument, and treating a popular belief as proof.
Creative writing works from imagination rather than from reporting. Its forms include the short story, the poem, a scene from a play, and the descriptive or reflective sketch. It may invent people, places and events outright, and it foregrounds voice, imagery, rhythm and structure. Freedom from fact is not freedom from craft: the invented world must obey its own rules, so a character cannot suddenly know what the story has not allowed them to know, and a shift in time must be signalled. Dialogue should sound like speech and do work—revealing character or moving the story on—rather than repeat what the narration has already said. A poem’s line breaks and a play’s stage directions are part of the meaning, not decoration. Choose the form the task asks for: a story needs a shape with a turn in it, a poem needs a pattern of sound, and a scene needs conflict between speakers. The narrative essay and the short story can share a structure; the difference is that the essay usually recounts a real or realistic experience in order to draw a lesson, while creative writing may invent throughout and cares most about how the telling works. Many tasks combine purposes—a story may need description, and an account may need explanation—so decide the dominant purpose and let the others serve it.
A formal report is a factual account written for someone in authority who was not present: a Principal, a head of department, a club patron or an outside body. Typical occasions are an accident or injury, a theft or other loss, the proceedings of a meeting, the work of a camp or committee, and a complaint or petition. Three habits separate a report from an essay. It sticks to facts that can be checked and marks clearly any statement that is not established. It is written for a reader who has to act, so it is orderly, brief and specific about times, places, people and amounts. It keeps opinion out of the account and puts any recommendation in its own section, and then only where a recommendation was asked for. Past tenses carry the events, and reported speech carries what other people said.
Follow the layout of a formal letter, then build the report inside it. Write your own address block, with your class or office and the date. Write the recipient’s name, designation and address. Add the salutation “Sir” or “Madam”. Give the report a heading that states its subject, such as “Report on the theft of laboratory equipment”. Then number the sections of the body: terms of reference, saying who asked for the report and why; an account of what happened, answering when, where, who and what, in order; findings or causes; action already taken; and recommendations, if they were requested. Close with “Yours faithfully”, then your signature, your full name and the office you hold. Reported speech is the part most often got wrong. When you report what someone said, move the verb one step back in time, change the pronouns, and change time and place words: “I locked the gate yesterday” becomes he said that he had locked the gate the day before, and “we will meet here tomorrow” becomes they said that they would meet there the following day. Keep a direct quotation only where the exact words matter, and then punctuate it as a quotation. Do not mix the two forms in one sentence.
Minutes are the official record of a meeting: who attended, what was considered, what was decided and who must act. A meeting is announced by a notice that carries the agenda, the list of items to be discussed, so the minutes follow the agenda’s order. Write them in this sequence: the name of the organisation and the kind of meeting; the date, time and venue; the presiding officer; the members present, and those absent with apologies; the opening, naming who opened it; the reading and confirmation of the previous minutes, with any correction; matters arising from those minutes; then each agenda item in turn, recording what was considered and the decision reached; any other business; the time of adjournment and the date of the next meeting; and finally the signatures of the Chairperson and the Secretary. Use the past tense and the third person, and report what was said rather than quoting it at length. Record a decision as a resolution with the person responsible and the deadline, because a minute that records only discussion leaves nothing to act on. Leave out your own opinions, jokes and verbatim dialogue, and do not invent an attendance or a decision to fill a gap. The source page begins the minutes with the club name, date, venue and list of members and then stops; the order above completes what it leaves out.
Here is a model. It is invented for practice. The Literary and Debating Society of Bright Star Secondary School held its second meeting of the term on Thursday, 4 February 2027 at 2.00 p.m. in the Assembly Hall. The Chairperson, Ada Nwosu, presided, and the Secretary, Ibrahim Sule, recorded the minutes. Twelve members were present and three sent apologies. The Chairperson opened the meeting with a prayer, and the minutes of the previous meeting were read and confirmed without amendment. Under matters arising, the Secretary reported that the notice board promised at the last meeting had not yet been bought. The Society then resolved that the inter-house debate would hold on 25 February 2027 on the motion “Boarding school is better than day school”, and a committee of three was asked to prepare the topics and invite two teachers to judge, reporting to the Secretary by 11 February. On the request for a notice board, the Treasurer was asked to obtain prices and report at the next meeting, and the Society agreed to spend no more than fifteen thousand naira, subject to the Principal’s approval. There was no other business. The meeting was adjourned at 3.20 p.m., and the next meeting will be on 18 February 2027 at 2.00 p.m. in the same venue. The minutes were signed by Ada Nwosu, Chairperson, and Ibrahim Sule, Secretary. When you answer a question of this kind, work in four steps: read the facts you were given and list them under the required headings; draft the opening details before anything else; record each agenda item with its decision, the person responsible and the date; then check the tense, the third person and the signatures. For a report, check in the same way against the layout, and make sure every reported statement has been moved back one tense.

practice.question: Name the essay type that each instruction calls for: (1) “Describe the market on a busy Saturday morning.” (2) “Explain how water is treated before it reaches homes.” (3) “Argue for or against the wearing of school uniforms.” (4) “Write a story that ends with the words I should have listened.” (5) “Narrate an incident that taught you the value of patience.” (6) “Set out the steps a club should follow to organise a clean-up exercise.”
practice.answer: (1) descriptive; (2) expository, using the process pattern; (3) argumentative; (4) creative writing, in the form of a short story; (5) narrative; (6) expository, using the process pattern.

practice.question: For each topic, choose the most suitable essay type and give one reason based on the writer’s purpose. (1) The advantages and disadvantages of using mobile phones in school. (2) A day I will never forget. (3) Why our town needs a public library. (4) My grandmother’s kitchen.
practice.answer: (1) Expository, using comparison and contrast, because the writer must set out both sides evenly rather than defend one. (2) Narrative, because the writer recounts a sequence of events and draws a lesson from it. (3) Argumentative, because the writer must defend a claim that the town needs a library and answer objection to it. (4) Descriptive, because the writer must create an impression of a place through ordered sensory detail.

marking.criterion: (1) reason: purpose is to set out both sides, not to persuade
(2) reason: purpose is to recount events and draw a lesson
(3) reason: purpose is to defend a claim against objection
(4) reason: purpose is to create an impression of a place through sensory detail

practice.question: These narrative stages are in random order: climax; resolution; setting and characters; final reflection; complication; opening situation. Write them in a workable order from first to last.
practice.answer: (1) setting and characters; (2) opening situation; (3) complication; (4) climax; (5) resolution; (6) final reflection.

practice.question: For each topic write (a) a claim that could reasonably be disputed, (b) one reason with a supporting example, (c) one likely counterargument, and (d) a brief rebuttal. Topic A: school should start later in the morning. Topic B: social media does more harm than good to students.
practice.answer: Topic A. (a) Claim: secondary school should begin at 8.30 a.m. rather than 7.30 a.m. (b) Reason: students who begin later are more alert in the first lessons; for example, a class that has eaten breakfast follows instructions without repeated reminders. (c) Counterargument: a later start leaves less time for afternoon lessons and extra-curricular activities. (d) Rebuttal: repeated revision periods can be shortened, so the teaching day is preserved without starting so early. Topic B. (a) Claim: students should limit social media to one hour a day. (b) Reason: time lost to scrolling reduces study and sleep; for example, a student who checks messages at midnight arrives tired. (c) Counterargument: social media helps students share schoolwork and keep in touch with family. (d) Rebuttal: a fixed limit keeps those benefits while preventing the late-night use that harms study and sleep.

marking.criterion: Topic A (a) a disputable claim about a later start
Topic A (b) one reason supported by a specific example
Topic A (c) a counterargument stated fairly, not as a straw man
Topic A (d) a rebuttal that answers that counterargument
Topic B (a) a disputable claim about students’ social media use
Topic B (b) one reason supported by a specific example
Topic B (c) a counterargument stated fairly, not as a straw man
Topic B (d) a rebuttal that answers that counterargument

practice.question: Number these parts of a formal report from 1 to 10 in the order they should appear: account of what happened; closing “Yours faithfully”; heading or title; recipient’s name, designation and address; recommendations; salutation; signature, full name and office held; terms of reference; findings or causes; writer’s address and date.
practice.answer: 1 writer’s address and date; 2 recipient’s name, designation and address; 3 salutation; 4 heading or title; 5 terms of reference; 6 account of what happened; 7 findings or causes; 8 recommendations; 9 closing “Yours faithfully”; 10 signature, full name and office held.

marking.criterion: (10) signature, full name and office held

practice.question: Convert each direct statement into reported speech for a formal report. (1) The caretaker said, “I locked the gate at six o’clock yesterday.” (2) A witness said, “The two boys ran towards the market.” (3) The Principal said, “I will announce the new rule tomorrow.”
practice.answer: (1) The caretaker said that he had locked the gate at six o’clock the day before. (2) A witness said that the two boys had run towards the market. (3) The Principal said that he would announce the new rule the following day.

marking.criterion: (1) pronoun and time word changed: he, the day before
(2) reported as a statement with that (the tense of ran becomes had run)
(3) pronoun and time word changed: he, the following day

practice.question: Write the minutes of the meeting described here. Use the correct order and the past tense, name the presiding officer and the secretary, and record each decision with the person responsible. Harmony Secondary School Science Club met on Tuesday, 9 March 2027 at 3.00 p.m. in the Chemistry Laboratory. The Chairperson, Musa Bello, presided, and the Secretary, Grace Eze, kept the record. Fifteen members were present and two sent apologies. The agenda was: opening; reading and confirmation of the previous minutes; preparation for the science fair; request for a first-aid box; any other business; adjournment. The previous minutes were confirmed without amendment. The club resolved that the science fair would take place on 24 March 2027 and that each group would submit its project title to the Secretary by 16 March. The club also agreed to ask the school nurse to teach basic first aid on 18 March and to spend eight thousand naira from club dues on a first-aid box, which the Treasurer would buy before that session. There was no other business. The meeting was adjourned at 4.10 p.m., and the next meeting is on 23 March 2027 at 3.00 p.m. in the same venue.
practice.answer: Model minutes. HARMONY SECONDARY SCHOOL SCIENCE CLUB: MINUTES OF THE MEETING HELD ON TUESDAY, 9 MARCH 2027. The meeting of the Harmony Secondary School Science Club was held on Tuesday, 9 March 2027 at 3.00 p.m. in the Chemistry Laboratory. The Chairperson, Musa Bello, presided, and the Secretary, Grace Eze, recorded the minutes. Fifteen members were present; two members sent apologies. The Chairperson opened the meeting and the minutes of the previous meeting were read and confirmed without amendment. Under preparation for the science fair, the club resolved that the fair would take place on 24 March 2027, and each group was asked to submit its project title to the Secretary by 16 March 2027. On the request for a first-aid box, the club resolved to ask the school nurse to teach basic first aid on 18 March 2027 and to spend eight thousand naira from club dues on a first-aid box; the Treasurer was asked to buy the box before that session. There was no other business. The meeting was adjourned at 4.10 p.m.; the next meeting will be held on 23 March 2027 at 3.00 p.m. in the Chemistry Laboratory. Signed: Musa Bello, Chairperson, and Grace Eze, Secretary.

marking.criterion: Names the club, the kind of meeting and the date
Gives the time, the venue and the presiding officer
Records attendance and apologies, naming the Secretary
Records that the previous minutes were read and confirmed without amendment
Science fair: date of 24 March and the project-title deadline of 16 March, submitted to the Secretary
First aid: nurse’s session on 18 March, eight thousand naira approved and the Treasurer asked to buy the box
Records the adjournment time, the next meeting and the signatures

practice.question: A pupil wrote these draft minutes. Identify three faults that would be marked wrong in an examination and correct each one. Draft: “The meeting started at 3 p.m. I welcome all members. The club decide to hold the fair on 24 March. The treasurer buys the box.”
practice.answer: (1) First person: minutes are written in the third person, so “I welcome all members” becomes “The Chairperson welcomed all members.” (2) Present tense for a meeting already held: “The club decide” becomes “The club resolved” or “The club decided”. (3) A decision with no action recorded: “The treasurer buys the box” becomes “The Treasurer was asked to buy the first-aid box before 18 March.”

marking.criterion: Fault 1 corrected to the third person
Fault 2 identified: present tense for a past meeting
Fault 2 corrected to a past-tense verb
Fault 3 identified: decision recorded without the action, agent and deadline
Fault 3 corrected as an action point naming who acts and by when

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Idioms: fixed form, reviewed meanings and use in sentences
objectives: Define an idiom and use the tests of compositionality, fixedness and limited variation to tell an idiom from an ordinary phrase.

Write the fixed form of common idioms correctly, including take the bull by the horns, at a snail’s pace, throw light on, call a halt to, breathe one’s last, birds of a feather and have light fingers.
Give the meaning of idioms of difficulty, character, conflict, effort and daily life in a full phrase and use each in a sentence where the meaning is clear.
Recognise expressions that are not idioms, such as a backlog, ample opportunity and the beginning of a new era, and explain why.
Use idioms sparingly and in the right register, without mixing images or altering the grammar of the fixed phrase.
Correct the four recurring faults in idiom answers: the half-remembered singular, the wrong part of speech, the dropped possessive and the phrase that was never an idiom.
lessons.body:
An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be worked out from its words one by one. “He shed crocodile tears” does not describe a reptile: it says that his sorrow was pretended. Because the meaning belongs to the whole phrase, an idiom has to be learned as a unit—the words, the meaning, and one example sentence that shows the meaning in use. Three tests help you recognise one. Composition: the meaning is not the sum of the parts. Fixedness: the words cannot be swapped for near-synonyms, so “kick the bucket” does not become “kick the pail”. Limited variation: an article or a plural may be fixed, as in “at a snail’s pace” or “birds of a feather”. Idioms are common in speech, in journalism and in informal writing. In a formal report or an examination essay, use them sparingly and only where the meaning is exact.
Most of the wording errors in the source list are errors of fixed form, so learn the whole phrase and mark the part that never changes. The idiom is to take the bull by the horns, not by the horn, because the plural is fixed. The pace is at a snail’s pace, with the possessive and the preposition: the work went on at a snail’s pace. To throw light needs its preposition—throw light on a problem. The standard phrase is call a halt to something, with the object after the preposition. To breathe one’s last has breathe as its verb; the source’s “the breathe” confuses the verb with the noun breath. The proverb is birds of a feather flock together, so the phrase is birds of a feather, not a bird of a feather, and it describes people of the same kind. To have light fingers, in the plural, means to be inclined to steal. Burn the candle at both ends keeps its article and its plural. Learning the correct form first prevents the commonest examination error, which is a half-remembered phrase.
Idioms for difficulty and endurance. An acid test is a decisive test of the value or quality of something: the trial match was an acid test of the new formation. A baptism of fire is a first experience that is difficult or dangerous: her first week in the emergency ward was a baptism of fire. A situation of ease is a bed of roses, and the idiom is almost always used in the negative—running a school is not a bed of roses. To be at a low ebb is to be in a poor or declining state: his confidence was at a low ebb after the defeat. To be at sixes and sevens is to be in confusion or disorder: the files were at sixes and sevens after the move. To be at a crossroads is to be at a point where a decision must be made: the club is at a crossroads. To be in the same boat is to face the same difficulties as someone else: both teams were in the same boat after the rain.
Idioms for people and character. A wet blanket is a person who discourages others or spoils their enjoyment: do not be a wet blanket about the trip. An Achilles’ heel is a person’s weak point: arithmetic is his Achilles’ heel. To have light fingers is to be inclined to steal. To blow one’s own trumpet is to praise oneself: he blew his own trumpet throughout the interview. To be tied to someone’s apron strings is to depend on that person more than is healthy, and it is usually used of a child or a husband. A captain of industry is a leading figure in business: the hall was built by a captain of industry. To play to the gallery is to act in order to win cheap popular approval rather than to do what is right. Birds of a feather are people of the same kind, and the full proverb adds that they flock together, which is why the phrase is often used as a warning about the company someone keeps.
Idioms for conflict and peace. To bury the hatchet is to end a quarrel and make peace: the two families buried the hatchet at the wedding. To hold out an olive branch is to show that one wants peace or agreement. An apple of discord is a cause of disagreement: the choice of venue became an apple of discord. To add insult to injury is to make a bad situation worse by an additional offence: the shop was closed, and to add insult to injury it began to rain. To do something in cold blood is to do it deliberately and without pity. To bring someone to their knees is to force them into submission. Notice that each of these phrases carries a judgement, so a report that must stay neutral should describe the events and keep the idiom for a comment, if it uses one at all.
Idioms for effort and ambition. To burn the midnight oil is to work or study late into the night: she burned the midnight oil before the examination. To burn the candle at both ends is to exhaust oneself by combining late nights with early mornings. To blaze a trail is to be the first to do something and so show others the way: the school blazed a trail in teaching coding. To build castles in the air is to make plans or hopes that are unlikely to come true. By hook or by crook means by any means available, and it carries a warning because the means may not be fair. By rule of thumb means by a rough method based on practice rather than theory: by rule of thumb, one supervisor is needed for every twenty pupils. A related phrase is to chase shadows, which means to pursue something that cannot be caught; the source gloss “to deceive oneself” does not fit the way the phrase is used.
Idioms for money and daily life. To live from hand to mouth is to spend money as it comes, with nothing saved. A stone’s throw is a short distance: the market is a stone’s throw from the gate. To be at a loose end is to have nothing to do: I was at a loose end on Saturday. To be behind closed doors is to be in private, with no outsider present: the committee met behind closed doors. To draw the line is to set a limit beyond which one will not go: we allow late work once, but we draw the line there. To nip something in the bud is to stop it before it develops: the teacher nipped the quarrel in the bud. To water something down is to weaken it: the proposal was watered down before it was approved. To catch someone’s eye is to attract their attention. First-hand information comes from the original source, and the compound takes a hyphen when it comes before a noun: first-hand information, but information obtained first hand.
Some of the expressions in the source list are not idioms, and calling them idioms teaches the wrong test. A backlog is a single noun with its own dictionary sense: an accumulation of unfinished work or of arrears. Ample opportunity is an ordinary quantifier with a noun, meaning simply plenty of chance, and its meaning is the sum of its words. The beginning of a new era is an ordinary descriptive phrase of the same kind. An airy nothing is a literary phrase, not a set expression in general use, and it should not be presented to learners as an idiom. You can decide for yourself with the composition test: if you can work out the meaning from the words, you are reading ordinary language, not an idiom. A second warning follows from this. A phrase may be figurative and still not be an idiom—weather metaphors such as “a storm of protest” are figures of speech, not fixed expressions with a stored meaning.
Use idioms as seasoning, not as the meal. One or two in a paragraph is enough; a page of them reads as though the writer is performing. Match the register: “in cold blood” suits a serious account, while “at a loose end” is conversational and sits badly in an official report. Do not mix two idioms that pull in different directions, and do not change the grammar around a fixed phrase. Here is a short model paragraph. “The committee met behind closed doors because the dispute had become an apple of discord. Both sides were in the same boat, and after two hours they agreed to bury the hatchet. The secretary, who hates meetings, was at a loose end only when the agenda ran out.” Each idiom keeps its fixed form, and each meaning is clear from the sentence without being explained.
Work in four steps when an idiom appears in a test. First, read the whole sentence and decide whether the phrase is literal or idiomatic; if the literal reading is absurd, the idiomatic one is intended. Second, recall the meaning of the whole phrase and state it in a full phrase rather than a single word, because most idioms carry a judgement that one word loses. Third, check the fixed form before you write: the article, the plural and the preposition are the three places where marks are lost. Fourth, write a sentence in which the meaning is visible from the situation, not from a definition tacked on. Four traps recur in this topic. The half-remembered singular gives “take a bull by the horn” for take the bull by the horns. The wrong part of speech gives “the breathe” for to breathe one’s last. The dropped possessive gives “a snail pace” for at a snail’s pace. And the phrase that was never an idiom gives “a backlog” for arrears. Checking the form and then the meaning catches all four.

practice.question: Match each idiom to its meaning. Idioms: (1) an acid test, (2) a wet blanket, (3) to bury the hatchet, (4) at a loose end, (5) a stone’s throw, (6) to nip something in the bud, (7) in cold blood, (8) to blow one’s own trumpet. Meanings: A to stop something before it grows; B a decisive test of quality; C with nothing to do; D to praise oneself; E deliberately and without pity; F a person who discourages others; G a short distance; H to end a quarrel.

marking.criterion: (1) B, a decisive test of quality
(2) F, a person who discourages others
(6) A, to stop something before it grows

practice.question: Complete each idiom with the missing word or words: (1) take the bull by the ____, (2) at a snail’s ____, (3) throw light ____ the problem, (4) call a ____ to the practice, (5) breathe one’s ____, (6) birds of a ____, (7) burn the candle at both ____, (8) have light ____.
practice.answer: (1) horns; (2) pace; (3) on; (4) halt; (5) last; (6) feather; (7) ends; (8) fingers.

practice.question: Each expression below is written in a faulty form. Write the correct form and give a one-line reason. (1) to take a bull by the horn; (2) a snail pace; (3) the breathe one’s last; (4) to call to a halt.
practice.answer: (1) to take the bull by the horns, because the definite article and the plural are fixed. (2) at a snail’s pace, because the possessive and the preposition are part of the idiom. (3) to breathe one’s last, because breathe is the verb and breath is the noun. (4) to call a halt to something, because the object follows the preposition to.

marking.criterion: (1) correct form: to take the bull by the horns
(2) correct form: at a snail’s pace
(3) correct form: to breathe one’s last
(3) reason: breathe is the verb, breath the noun
(4) correct form: to call a halt to something

practice.question: Use each idiom in a sentence of your own that makes its meaning clear: (1) a wet blanket, (2) to nip something in the bud, (3) at a loose end, (4) to bury the hatchet.
practice.answer: Model answers: (1) Nobody invited him to the planning meeting because he is such a wet blanket about every new idea. (2) The prefect nipped the name-calling in the bud before it spread through the class. (3) With no homework and no practice, she was at a loose end all afternoon. (4) The two brothers buried the hatchet and shared the work on the farm. Any sentence that keeps the fixed form and shows the meaning earns the marks.

marking.criterion: (1) idiom used in its fixed form
(2) idiom used in its fixed form
(3) idiom used in its fixed form
(4) idiom used in its fixed form

practice.question: Three of these six expressions are not idioms. Identify each one and give a reason: a backlog; an acid test; ample opportunity; a stone’s throw; the beginning of a new era; in cold blood.
practice.answer: A backlog: a single noun with its own dictionary sense, an accumulation of unfinished work or arrears. Ample opportunity: an ordinary quantifier with a noun, meaning plenty of chance, and its meaning is the sum of its words. The beginning of a new era: an ordinary descriptive phrase whose meaning can be worked out word by word. The other three are idioms: an acid test, a stone’s throw and in cold blood each carry a stored meaning that the words alone do not give.

marking.criterion: Identifies a backlog as not an idiom
Reason for a backlog: one noun with its own dictionary sense
Identifies ample opportunity as not an idiom
Reason for ample opportunity: ordinary quantifier plus noun, meaning is the sum of the words
Identifies the beginning of a new era as not an idiom
Reason for the beginning of a new era: ordinary descriptive phrase

practice.question: For each idiom, give its meaning in a full phrase and one sentence that shows the meaning: (1) a bed of roses, (2) a baptism of fire, (3) an acid test, (4) at a low ebb, (5) a captain of industry.
practice.answer: Model answers: (1) a situation of ease and comfort, almost always used in the negative—Looking after four younger children is not a bed of roses. (2) a first experience that is difficult or dangerous—His first day on the busy ward was a baptism of fire. (3) a decisive test of value or quality—The final match was an acid test of the team’s fitness. (4) in a poor or declining state—Morale was at a low ebb after the third defeat. (5) a leading figure in business—The library was funded by a captain of industry from the town. Accept any wording of the meaning that keeps the sense, with a sentence in which the idiom fits.

marking.criterion: (1) meaning of a bed of roses
(2) meaning of a baptism of fire
(4) meaning of at a low ebb
(5) meaning of a captain of industry

practice.question: Replace the bracketed words with a suitable idiom, keeping the sentence grammatical: (1) The manager [praised himself] throughout the meeting. (2) The two neighbours [stopped quarrelling] after the elders intervened. (3) She [works late into the night] before every examination. (4) The girl is [too dependent on her mother].
practice.answer: (1) The manager blew his own trumpet throughout the meeting. (2) The two neighbours buried the hatchet after the elders intervened. (3) She burns the midnight oil before every examination. (4) The girl is tied to her mother’s apron strings.

marking.criterion: (4) tied to her mother’s apron strings

practice.question: Write a short paragraph of three or four sentences about preparing for an examination, using three of these idioms correctly: to burn the midnight oil; at a loose end; a bed of roses; to nip something in the bud.
practice.answer: Model answer: Preparation is not a bed of roses, but it need not be a rush at the end. I burn the midnight oil for two evenings only, and I stop early on the night before the paper. Last term I was at a loose end for a whole week, so this term I nipped the habit in the bud. Any paragraph that uses three of the idioms in their fixed forms, with the meaning clear from the context, earns the marks.
