lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Entertainment vocabulary: sport and the theatre, with reviewed glosses
objectives: Name the athletics words in the source list and give a gloss that states the class of thing each word is.
Use the football words correctly, including the corrected gloss for football and the duties of referee and linesman.
Use the theatre words correctly, including the corrected gloss for curtain-call and the roles of actor, cast, director and usher.
Correct the four faulty source glosses: “wooden clothes” for track suit, the training gloss for athletics, the repeated clause for linesman, and the empty football entry.
Use the words in natural collocations and in other parts of speech, such as to referee, to usher and to cast.
Distinguish easily confused pairs: football and soccer, referee and linesman, actor and cast, and penalty and punishment.
lessons.body:
This lesson builds the vocabulary of entertainment in two of its main fields, sport and the theatre. It also reviews the glosses that the source page gives, because several of them need correction: one word has no gloss at all, one gloss repeats itself, and one describes an athlete’s clothing as wooden. A gloss is only useful if it gives the meaning in a full phrase and names the class of thing the word is—a person, an official, a place, an object or an event. Learn each word with three things: its meaning, its class, and one short sentence that uses it in a typical way. The words in this lesson divide neatly. Sport gives us events and distances, officials, players and equipment; the theatre gives us performers, the people who work around them, the places where the public is served, and one ritual that ends the evening.
Athletics is the name for track and field sports: running, jumping and throwing events such as sprints, relays, the long jump and the discus. The source gloss, “exercise of physical strength or speed”, describes training rather than the sport, so learn the category instead. A contingent is a group that forms part of a larger gathering; a school sends a contingent of athletes to a state competition, just as a regiment sends a contingent to a parade. A marathon is a long-distance running race, traditionally about forty-two kilometres, and the word is also used figuratively for anything long or exhausting: a marathon meeting. A podium is the raised platform on which the first three finishers stand to receive their medals; an athlete who finishes third is on the podium, and the verb phrase is to mount the podium. A track suit is warm clothing worn by athletes before and after exercise. The source gloss, “wooden clothes”, is a typing error for warm clothing, and the usual British spelling is two words, track suit, though tracksuit also appears.
Football is the game in which two teams of eleven players try to kick a ball into the other team’s goal, and soccer is a common British name for the same game; the source marks soccer as colloquial, which is right, because the word is informal. In British English, football is the ordinary name; in the United States the same game is called soccer, while football there means a different sport, so a sentence about football needs its context. The pitch is the field of play, not the field of a farm, and a match is played over two halves. Vocabulary that belongs with the game includes goal, goalkeeper, defender, midfielder, striker, offside, free kick, corner and the two officials below. A pupil writing about a match needs the players’ roles and the officials’ decisions, not only the name of the game.
Two officials control the game. The referee is the official in charge: he or she applies the rules, keeps time, cautions or sends off players, and awards free kicks and penalties. A linesman is an official who assists the referee, chiefly by judging whether the ball has left the field over a touchline or a goal line and which team should restart play. The neutral term assistant referee is now preferred in official use, and British football uses it in place of linesman; both words are correct in school writing, and the neutral one is safer in a formal report. The source gloss for linesman repeats the clause “the ball touches or crosses” twice; the corrected single clause is the one above. A penalty is a free kick at goal awarded for a serious foul inside the penalty area, and the verb is to concede or to take a penalty. Do not confuse the referee with the umpire, who controls sports such as tennis, cricket and hockey; football and athletics officials are referees or judges, not umpires.
The theatre has its own set of people words. An actor is a performer who takes a role in a play or a film, and the word is used for any gender, though actress is still used for women. A cast is the group of performers in a play or film: the whole cast came on stage to take a bow. The director is the person who shapes the production—choosing the cast, planning the staging and deciding how the text should be spoken. The usher is a member of staff who shows members of the audience to their seats and often hands out programmes. Notice how the four words divide: the actor performs, the cast is the group, the director decides, and the usher serves the audience. A theatre also needs a stage, wings, a curtain, scenery, costumes and lighting, though those words are not in this week’s list and can be learned with them.
Two more theatre words belong with the public side of the evening. The box-office is the theatre office or counter where seats are booked and tickets are bought; a play that sells well is described as a box-office success, and the expression has moved into general use for anything popular. A curtain-call is the return of the performers to the stage after the play, in answer to the audience’s applause; the source gloss explains the audience’s call but leaves out the performers’ return, and it is the return that the word chiefly names. The usual pattern is to take a curtain-call, and the whole cast takes one together. Note the difference between a curtain-call and a call to the audience for silence or for an encore: only the first is the fixed theatre term.
Most of these words also work as other parts of speech, and knowing the pattern is what turns recognition into use. Referee and usher are both verbs: to referee a match, to usher someone to a seat. Cast is a verb as well as a noun: the director cast the play, and the cast took a bow. Podium has no verb, but it has a fixed phrase, on the podium. Marathon becomes an adjective of sorts in a marathon meeting, a marathon session. Podium, cast and box-office each combine with common verbs: mount the podium, join the cast, book at the box-office. Learn the collocation with the word, because examination sentences are marked on whether the word sits naturally: a referee blows a whistle and awards a penalty; an usher shows you to a seat; a director casts the play.
Several words in this field are easily confused, and one or two are misdescribed in the source. Football and soccer name the same game in British English, but soccer is informal and football carries a different meaning in North America. Referee and linesman are not interchangeable: the referee is in charge, and the linesman assists. Actor and cast are not interchangeable either, because one is a person and the other is a group. A penalty is not the same as a punishment in general: it is a specific restart awarded for a foul in the penalty area, which is why the word appears in the laws of the game. Track suit is clothing and a running track is the place; the source’s “wooden clothes” gloss confuses the word with nothing at all and must be replaced. Curtain-call is not the interval, which is the break in the middle of a performance.
Use the vocabulary in whole sentences, because a list of words with one-word glosses does not show that a learner can use them. Some models: The school sent a contingent of twelve athletes to the zonal games. She finished third, so she mounted the podium to collect her bronze medal. The referee awarded a penalty after the defender handled the ball. The assistant referee raised his flag for offside. The whole cast took a curtain-call while the audience clapped. Tickets are sold at the box-office from nine in the morning. In a report on a school event, these words should carry the factual account—who took part, who officiated, what was decided—while the commentary stays in the report’s recommendation section. In an essay about entertainment, the same words support description, as in a crowded theatre where the ushers moved along the aisles.
When a vocabulary question appears in a test, work in four steps. First, name the class of thing the word is: person, official, place, object, group or event. Second, give the meaning in a full phrase that would still make sense to someone who has never met the word; do not define it by repeating it, since “a referee is a person who referees” says nothing. Third, add one typical collocation or sentence, because the collocation proves the meaning. Fourth, check the corrections in this lesson: athletics is a group of sports and not simple exercise; a track suit is warm clothing; a linesman assists the referee and judges whether the ball has crossed a line; and a curtain-call is the performers’ return to the stage. Those four points are where the source page would mislead a learner who studied it alone.

practice.question: Match each word to its gloss. Words: (1) athletics, (2) contingent, (3) marathon, (4) podium, (5) track suit, (6) linesman, (7) penalty, (8) referee, (9) box-office, (10) usher. Glosses: A the official in charge of a match; B a free kick at goal given for a serious foul; C track and field sports; D the theatre counter where seats are booked; E a group forming part of a larger gathering; F a raised platform for winners; G a member of staff who shows people to their seats; H warm clothing worn by athletes before and after exercise; I an official who assists the referee, chiefly on whether the ball has crossed a line; J a long-distance race.

marking.criterion: (2) E, a group forming part of a larger gathering
(4) F, a raised platform for winners
(5) H, warm clothing worn by athletes
(6) I, an official who assists the referee
(7) B, a free kick at goal given for a serious foul
(8) A, the official in charge of a match
(9) D, the theatre counter where seats are booked
(10) G, a member of staff who shows people to their seats

practice.question: Write the word that fits each description: (1) the group of performers in a play or film; (2) a member of staff who shows members of the audience to their seats; (3) the theatre office where tickets are bought; (4) the performers’ return to the stage in answer to applause; (5) the person who shapes the production and chooses the cast; (6) a raised platform on which winners stand; (7) a long-distance running race; (8) a group that forms part of a larger gathering.
practice.answer: (1) cast; (2) usher; (3) box-office; (4) curtain-call; (5) director; (6) podium; (7) marathon; (8) contingent.

practice.question: Each gloss below is faulty. Write a corrected gloss and give a one-line reason. (1) “Track suit: wooden clothes worn by athletes.” (2) “Athletics: exercise of physical strength or speed.” (3) “Linesman: an official who assists the referee, especially by deciding whether the ball touches or crosses the ball touches or crosses the line.” (4) “Football:” (no gloss given).
practice.answer: (1) A track suit is warm clothing worn by athletes before and after exercise; “wooden clothes” is a typing error and describes nothing. (2) Athletics is track and field sports: running, jumping and throwing events; the gloss describes training, not the sport. (3) A linesman is an official who assists the referee, chiefly by judging whether the ball has crossed a touchline or goal line; the source clause is repeated twice and must be given once. (4) Football is the game in which two teams of eleven players try to kick a ball into the other team’s goal; the source leaves the entry empty.

marking.criterion: (1) corrected gloss: warm clothing worn by athletes
(1) reason: the source gloss is a typing error
(2) corrected gloss: track and field sports
(2) reason: the source gloss describes training, not the sport
(3) corrected gloss: judges whether the ball has crossed a line
(3) reason: the source clause is repeated
(4) reason: the source entry has no gloss

practice.question: Use each word in a sentence of your own that shows its meaning: (1) podium, (2) penalty, (3) cast, (4) usher.
practice.answer: Model answers: (1) The winner stepped onto the podium to receive the trophy. (2) The referee awarded a penalty when the defender handled the ball in the area. (3) The whole cast came on stage for the final curtain-call. (4) An usher led us to our seats in the front row. Any sentence that uses the word in a natural collocation and shows the meaning earns the marks.

marking.criterion: (1) podium used with a natural collocation
(2) penalty used with a natural collocation
(3) cast used with a natural collocation
(4) usher used with a natural collocation

practice.question: Fill each gap with the correct word from this list: box-office, cast, linesman, marathon, podium, referee. (1) The race lasted forty-two kilometres, so it was a ____. (2) The winners stood together on the ____. (3) The ____ blew his whistle and stopped play. (4) The assistant ____ raised his flag because the ball had crossed the line. (5) Tickets for the play are sold at the ____. (6) The whole ____ came on stage at the end.
practice.answer: (1) marathon; (2) podium; (3) referee; (4) linesman; (5) box-office; (6) cast.

practice.question: Give the other part of speech named and use it in a sentence: (1) referee as a verb; (2) usher as a verb; (3) cast as a verb; (4) marathon as a word describing a long event.
practice.answer: Model answers: (1) to referee: Mr Bello refereed the final match. (2) to usher: The prefect ushered the visitors to their seats. (3) to cast: The director cast two new actors in the play. (4) a marathon event: The committee held a marathon meeting that ended at midnight.

marking.criterion: (4) marathon used for a long event

practice.question: Explain the difference between each pair and give one example of correct use: (1) football and soccer; (2) referee and linesman; (3) actor and cast; (4) penalty and punishment.
practice.answer: (1) Football is the ordinary British name for the game and also a different game in North America, while soccer is an informal British name for the same game; The school football team won the final. (2) The referee is in charge of the match and applies the rules, while the linesman assists, chiefly on whether the ball has crossed a line; The referee awarded a free kick and the linesman raised his flag. (3) An actor is one performer, while the cast is the whole group; One actor missed the rehearsal, but the rest of the cast attended. (4) A penalty is a specific free kick at goal for a foul in the area, while a punishment is any penalty imposed for an offence; The referee gave a penalty for the foul.

marking.criterion: (2) distinguishes the referee from the linesman
(3) distinguishes an actor from the cast
(4) distinguishes a penalty from punishment in general

practice.question: Write a paragraph of four to six sentences about either a school sports day or a school play. Use six of these words correctly: athletics, contingent, podium, referee, penalty, cast, curtain-call, box-office, usher.
practice.answer: Model answer about a play: Our school staged a play in the assembly hall, and the whole cast had rehearsed for three weeks. The ushers showed parents to their seats while tickets were checked at the box-office. The director watched from the back, and when the play ended the cast took a curtain-call that lasted several minutes. Any paragraph that uses six of the listed words in their correct senses and in natural sentences earns the marks.

marking.criterion: Word 1 used correctly in a natural sentence
Word 2 used correctly in a natural sentence
Word 3 used correctly in a natural sentence
Word 4 used correctly in a natural sentence
Word 5 used correctly in a natural sentence
Word 6 used correctly in a natural sentence

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Monophthongs: pure vowels and two examples of each sound
objectives: Define a monophthong as a pure vowel realised as a single element, and contrast it with a diphthong.
Identify the twelve British-English monophthongs by symbol.
Give two checked examples of each of the twelve monophthongs.
Classify a vowel sound as a monophthong or a diphthong.
Recognise that spelling is an unreliable guide to vowel sounds.
Use a dictionary check and an ordered method when answering an examples task.
lessons.body:
A monophthong is a vowel sound whose quality stays steady from beginning to end: the tongue, jaw and lips take up one position and hold it, so the sound is made of a single element. It is written with one phonemic symbol. A diphthong, by contrast, begins at one vowel quality and glides to another within the same syllable, which is why it is written with two symbols, as in /eɪ/ in day or /aʊ/ in now. Monophthongs are therefore called pure vowels. British English has twelve monophthongs and eight diphthongs.
The twelve monophthongs are /iː ɪ e æ ɑː ɒ ɔː ʊ uː ʌ ɜː ə/. They are usually grouped by relative length. The short vowels are /ɪ/ (kit), /e/ (dress), /æ/ (trap), /ɒ/ (lot), /ʊ/ (foot), /ʌ/ (strut) and /ə/ (comma). The long vowels are /iː/ (fleece), /ɑː/ (palm), /ɔː/ (thought), /uː/ (goose) and /ɜː/ (nurse). The length mark /ː/ is part of the symbol: /ɪ/ and /iː/ are different phonemes, so ship and sheep are not the same word. /ə/, the schwa, is the weak vowel of unstressed syllables and is never stressed.
The twelve sounds with two ordinary examples each: /iː/ see, team; /ɪ/ sit, big; /e/ bed, said; /æ/ cat, hand; /ɑː/ car, father; /ɒ/ hot, clock; /ɔː/ saw, door; /ʊ/ book, put; /uː/ food, blue; /ʌ/ cup, love; /ɜː/ bird, work; /ə/ about, teacher. Say each pair aloud and check that the vowel is held in one position. The examples are common words chosen so that the target sound falls in the stressed syllable, except for /ə/, which is always unstressed.
Letters are not sounds, so spelling is an unreliable guide. The same letter can stand for different vowels, as a in cat /æ/, car /ɑː/ and about /ə/; and the same sound can be written in different ways, as /iː/ in see, team and machine, or /ʌ/ in cup, love and blood. Silent letters change nothing: the final e in these is silent and the vowel is /iː/. Some letters have no vowel value at all, as in queue /kjuː/. A spelling rule such as 'two vowels together' cannot tell you which monophthong to use; only a dictionary or a reliable pronunciation model can.
Several pairs are easily confused because the symbols look alike. /ɪ/ and /iː/ differ in quality and length (ship/sheep, live/leave); /æ/ and /e/ differ mainly in the height of the tongue (bad/bed, man/men); /ɒ/ and /ɔː/ differ in length and rounding (cot/caught); /ʊ/ and /uː/ likewise (full/fool); /ʌ/ and /ɑː/ differ in both quality and length (cut/cart). The schwa /ə/ is not a stressed version of /ʌ/: above begins with /ə/ in British English, while cup has /ʌ/. Unstressed syllables in longer words often reduce to /ə/, as in the second syllable of support /səˈpɔːt/.
To decide whether a vowel is a monophthong or a diphthong, say the word slowly and notice whether the vowel stays in one place or moves. If the sound holds a single quality, it is a monophthong and one symbol describes it; if the tongue or lips visibly move during the vowel, it is a diphthong, as in boy /bɔɪ/, my /maɪ/ or go /ɡəʊ/. The written form can help only when it is a phonemic transcription. Ordinary spelling can hide a diphthong: the letter i in my and the letters ow in now are single vowel letters or digraphs but still represent gliding sounds.
When a question asks for two examples of each sound, work in a fixed order: symbol, then two words, then a check. Write all twelve symbols first so that none is missed. Choose common words that you can say confidently; do not repeat a word for two different vowels, and do not offer a spelling pattern in place of a word. Check each word in a dictionary that gives British pronunciation, and make sure the target vowel, not a neighbouring one, is the vowel of the stressed syllable. Where a word contains more than one vowel, name the syllable you are using. A model set of twelve pairs is given in the paragraph above and in practice Q1.
Written work can show that you know the symbols, the definitions and a set of checked examples. It cannot by itself prove that your mouth makes the contrast reliably, and no written key can certify listening or speaking. Those skills are assessed through oral observation with an authorised model, which is outside this written lesson. Use the practice below to test the written knowledge; treat pronunciation itself as a separate speaking task.

practice.question: Give two examples of each of the twelve monophthongs: /iː/, /ɪ/, /e/, /æ/, /ɑː/, /ɒ/, /ɔː/, /ʊ/, /uː/, /ʌ/, /ɜː/ and /ə/.
practice.answer: Model set, with one acceptable pair per sound: /iː/ see, team; /ɪ/ sit, big; /e/ bed, said; /æ/ cat, hand; /ɑː/ car, father; /ɒ/ hot, clock; /ɔː/ saw, door; /ʊ/ book, put; /uː/ food, blue; /ʌ/ cup, love; /ɜː/ bird, work; /ə/ about, teacher. Award the marks for any two words whose stressed vowel, checked in a British-pronunciation dictionary, is the symbol given; /ə/ words must have the schwa in an unstressed syllable. A word used for one vowel is not accepted again for another.

practice.question: Classify each sound as a monophthong or a diphthong: /eɪ/, /ɪ/, /ɔɪ/, /uː/, /əʊ/, /æ/, /aʊ/, /ɜː/, /eə/, /ɒ/.
practice.answer: Monophthongs: /ɪ/, /uː/, /æ/, /ɜː/, /ɒ/. Diphthongs: /eɪ/, /ɔɪ/, /əʊ/, /aʊ/, /eə/. Each monophthong is a single steady vowel quality written with one symbol; each diphthong glides between two qualities and is written with two symbols.

marking.criterion: the five monophthongs listed correctly (1 each)
the five diphthongs listed correctly (1 each)

practice.question: Write the vowel sound in the stressed syllable of each word: bread, move, rough, bird, watch, busy.
practice.answer: bread /e/; move /uː/; rough /ʌ/; bird /ɜː/; watch /ɒ/; busy /ɪ/. Bread is not /iː/ despite its spelling, move has /uː/ rather than /əʊ/, and busy has /ɪ/ although it is written with u.

practice.question: For each pair, write the vowel symbol of each word and name one difference: ship/sheep, bad/bed, full/fool, cot/caught.
practice.answer: ship /ɪ/ and sheep /iː/: /ɪ/ is shorter and slightly lower; bad /æ/ and bed /e/: /æ/ is lower, with the jaw more open; full /ʊ/ and fool /uː/: /ʊ/ is shorter and less rounded; cot /ɒ/ and caught /ɔː/: /ɒ/ is shorter and made with a more open jaw.

practice.question: Correct these three statements: (a) The word women begins with /uː/. (b) Said contains the diphthong /eɪ/. (c) Every vowel letter is pronounced with its alphabet name.
practice.answer: (a) Women begins with /ɪ/ (/wɪmɪn/). (b) Said contains the monophthong /e/ (/sed/), not the diphthong /eɪ/. (c) The statement is false: a vowel letter can stand for many sounds, and the letter a in cat is /æ/, not /eɪ/. One mark for each corrected statement and one mark for each reason.

marking.criterion: (a) /ɪ/ with the transcription or a word example
(c) statement rejected with a counter-example such as cat /æ/

practice.question: For each word, write the vowel symbol and say whether it is long or short: sit, seat, book, food, cup, cart.
practice.answer: sit /ɪ/, short; seat /iː/, long; book /ʊ/, short; food /uː/, long; cup /ʌ/, short; cart /ɑː/, long. The length mark /ː/ must be written for the long vowels.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Revision: reported speech, suffixation and the passive voice
objectives: Report statements accurately, with the correct backshift, pronouns and time and place words.
Report questions, commands and requests in statement order and with the correct infinitive.
Choose correctly between say and tell.
Form nouns and adjectives from bases with common suffixes, including -ment, and spell them correctly.
Convert active sentences into the passive across the tenses used in the syllabus.
Identify and correct errors in reported speech, suffixation and voice.
lessons.body:
This revision lesson brings together three structures that are tested together: reported speech, suffixation and the passive voice. They are different topics, but each rewards the same habits: identify the parts of the sentence, apply one rule at a time, and check the finished sentence against the meaning. The practice set below is original and every item has a worked answer, so the lesson can be studied without a teacher's key.
Reported speech tells someone what another person said without quoting the exact words. Direct speech keeps the speaker's words inside quotation marks: Ada said, 'I am tired.' Reported speech removes the quotation marks and usually introduces the words with that: Ada said that she was tired. The reporting clause (Ada said) frames the message; the reported clause carries the meaning. The meaning must stay the same even though the words change.
When the reporting verb is in the past, the verb in the reported clause usually moves one step back. Present simple becomes past simple; present continuous becomes past continuous; present perfect and past simple become past perfect; will becomes would; can becomes could; may becomes might; must expressing obligation becomes had to; shall becomes should. So 'I work here' becomes he said that he worked there, and 'I have finished' becomes she said that she had finished. A statement about a universal truth or a permanent fact may keep the present tense: the teacher said that water boils at 100 degrees. The backshift is a strong pattern, not a blind rule; the test is whether the time reference still makes sense.
Pronouns and time and place words change with the point of view. I and me usually become he, she, him or her; we becomes they; my becomes his or her; now becomes then; today becomes that day; tonight becomes that night; tomorrow becomes the next day or the following day; yesterday becomes the day before or the previous day; last week becomes the week before; here becomes there; this becomes that; ago becomes before. Change only what the new point of view requires: if the report is made in the same place on the same day, here and today may stay.
Say and tell are not interchangeable. Tell normally needs a person as its object: he told me the news; he told me that he was late. Say does not take a person as its direct object: he said that he was late, or he said to me that he was late, but not he said me that he was late. Reported questions keep the question word but use statement order: 'Where do you live?' becomes he asked me where I lived, not where did I live. A yes-or-no question is introduced by if or whether: she asked whether I had eaten. Reported commands and requests use tell or ask plus a person and a to-infinitive: the teacher told us to close the door; she asked him to help her; the negative is not to: he told us not to be late.
A suffix is a meaningful ending added to a base. It can change the word class. The suffix -ment forms nouns from verbs: endear becomes endearment, amaze becomes amazement, enjoy becomes enjoyment, and argue becomes argument, with the final e of argue dropped. The suffix -ness forms nouns from adjectives: happy becomes happiness, with y changed to i; kind becomes kindness. The suffixes -ful and -less form adjectives: care becomes careful and careless; hope becomes hopeful and hopeless. Other common suffixes are -tion (educate, education), -able (read, readable), -ly (quick, quickly) and -en (wide, widen). Check the spelling of each derived form rather than assuming the base is unchanged.
The passive voice changes the focus of a sentence from the doer to the receiver of the action. The active sentence the hunter killed the lion has the doer (the hunter) as subject and the receiver (the lion) as object. In the passive the receiver becomes the subject, the verb becomes a form of be plus the past participle, and the doer may be added with by: the lion was killed by the hunter. The by-phrase is omitted when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious: my bag was stolen. Only a transitive verb, one with an object, can be made passive; the baby slept has no passive because slept has no object.
The passive keeps the tense of the active. Present simple: the letters are delivered. Past simple: the letters were delivered. Present continuous: the letters are being delivered. Past continuous: the letters were being delivered. Present perfect: the letters have been delivered. Past perfect: the letters had been delivered. Future with will: the letters will be delivered. Modal: the letters can be delivered. Notice that the form of be carries the tense and the past participle never changes. A past participle is not the same as a past tense form: written, not wrote; broken, not broke; announced, not announce.
Some verbs take two objects, and either object may become the subject of a passive. They gave Ada a prize becomes Ada was given a prize or a prize was given to Ada. Choose the version that keeps the more natural focus; the person is often the better subject. In speech, get is sometimes used instead of be (the window got broken), but get is informal and should be avoided in formal writing. Do not use the passive to hide responsibility when the doer matters: the active sentence names who acted, and that may be exactly what the reader needs.
A revision method for all three topics. First, read the whole sentence and mark the subject, verb and object or message. Second, decide which rule applies: backshift and point of view for reporting, base plus suffix for word formation, or object-to-subject plus be and past participle for the passive. Third, write the whole sentence, not just the missing word, and read it back for meaning and spelling. Common errors to check are a missing object after tell, a reported question in question order, a forgotten backshift, a wrong past participle, an omitted -s or -ed, and a suffix that changes the spelling of the base. A written key can confirm these forms, but only a teacher can confirm that your explanation is clear; treat the answers below as models, not as the only possible correct wording where the question allows a choice.

practice.question: Report these statements in indirect speech, beginning with the words given. (a) 'I am tired,' Ada said. (Ada said ...) (b) 'We will come tomorrow,' they said. (They said ...) (c) 'I have finished the work,' he told me. (He told me ...) (d) 'My mother is cooking now,' she said. (She said ...) (e) 'I saw the film yesterday,' Tunde said. (Tunde said ...)
practice.answer: (a) Ada said that she was tired. (b) They said that they would come the next day. (c) He told me that he had finished the work. (d) She said that her mother was cooking then. (e) Tunde said that he had seen the film the day before. The conjunction that may be omitted in each answer; the reported clause must keep the meaning and the correct backshift.

marking.criterion: (a) pronoun she (1) and past tense was (1)
(b) would come (1) and next day or following day (1)
(c) had finished (1) and the person/object after told (1)
(d) was cooking (1) and then or at that time (1)
(e) had seen (1) and the day before or previous day (1)

practice.question: Report these questions and commands. (a) 'Where do you live?' he asked me. (b) 'Have you eaten?' she asked him. (c) 'Close the door,' the teacher told us. (d) 'Please help me,' she said to him.
practice.answer: (a) He asked me where I lived. (b) She asked him whether (or if) he had eaten. (c) The teacher told us to close the door. (d) She asked him to help her. Reported questions use statement order, and reported commands use tell or ask with a person and a to-infinitive.

marking.criterion: (a) where kept (1) and statement order I lived (1)
(b) if or whether (1) and past perfect had eaten (1)
(c) told us (1) and to close the door (1)
(d) asked him (1) and to help her with the pronoun (1)

practice.question: Correct the error in each sentence: (a) He told that he was tired. (b) She said me the answer. (c) The teacher asked me where did I live.
practice.answer: (a) He said that he was tired. Tell needs a person as object, and none is given. (b) She told me the answer. Say cannot take me directly as its object. (c) The teacher asked me where I lived. A reported question does not use the auxiliary did or question order.

practice.question: Add the suffix to the base, write the derived word, and name its word class: (a) endear + -ment; (b) amaze + -ment; (c) argue + -ment; (d) happy + -ness; (e) care + -ful; (f) hope + -less.
practice.answer: (a) endearment, noun. (b) amazement, noun. (c) argument, noun; the final e of argue is dropped. (d) happiness, noun; y changes to i. (e) careful, adjective. (f) hopeless, adjective.

practice.question: Rewrite each sentence in the passive voice, keeping the tense: (a) The hunter killed the lion. (b) They have repaired the road. (c) The committee will announce the results. (d) Someone stole my bag. (e) The teacher is marking the scripts. (f) They had finished the work before noon.
practice.answer: (a) The lion was killed by the hunter. (b) The road has been repaired. (c) The results will be announced by the committee. (d) My bag was stolen. (e) The scripts are being marked by the teacher. (f) The work had been finished before noon. The by-phrase may be omitted where the doer is unknown or unimportant, as in (b) and (d).

marking.criterion: (a) was killed with the object as subject
(b) has been repaired with the tense kept
(c) will be announced with the object as subject
(d) was stolen with the object as subject
(e) are being marked with the tense kept
(f) had been finished with the tense kept

practice.question: Answer briefly. (a) Name the voice of 'The letter was written by Ada.' (b) Turn 'The window was broken by the boys' into the active voice. (c) Explain why 'The baby slept' cannot be made passive. (d) Report this command: 'Bring the book,' she said to me. (e) Form a noun from amaze using -ment. (f) Correct 'The results were announce by the teacher.'
practice.answer: (a) Passive. (b) The boys broke the window. (c) Slept is intransitive and has no object, so there is nothing to become the subject of a passive sentence. (d) She told me (or asked me) to bring the book. (e) Amazement. (f) The results were announced by the teacher; the past participle announced is needed, not the base form.

marking.criterion: (c) intransitive or no object, so no passive subject
(d) told or asked me to bring the book

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Noun phrases and verb phrases: heads, non-finite phrases and functions
objectives: Define a noun phrase and identify a noun, pronoun or adjective as its head.
Identify the functions a noun phrase can perform in a sentence.
Explain gerund and infinitive phrases working as noun phrases.
Explain adjective-headed noun phrases and their agreement.
Identify the noun phrase that complements a preposition.
Identify verb phrases and name the function of bracketed noun-phrase and verb-phrase expressions.
lessons.body:
A noun phrase is a group of words built around a noun or a pronoun as its head. The head is the word that the other words modify and that decides what the phrase can do. In 'the two tall boys', the head is boys; in 'my best friend', it is friend. A single word can be a noun phrase: 'Dogs bark.' A pronoun can also be the head: 'They arrived late'; 'Everyone in the hall stood up' (head everyone); 'Those of us who stayed helped' (head those). The pronoun does the noun work, and any modifiers gather around it. This is why the definition names both a noun and a pronoun as possible heads.
A noun phrase can do the work of a noun in the sentence. As subject: 'The new bridge was opened yesterday.' As direct object: 'We visited the old market.' As indirect object, with a direct object after it: 'The teacher gave the class a test.' As subject complement, after a linking verb such as be, seem or become: 'My sister is a doctor.' As object complement, after the object it describes: 'They called the result a surprise' (a surprise describes the result). As complement of a preposition: 'We waited at the gate.'
A gerund is the -ing form of a verb used as a noun. A gerund phrase is the gerund together with its object or adverbial: 'Swimming in the sea is dangerous' (subject); 'She enjoys reading novels' (direct object); 'His hobby is collecting stamps' (subject complement); 'He is good at solving puzzles' (complement of the preposition at). The whole phrase is a noun phrase, so it can occupy any slot that a noun can occupy. Do not call the gerund a verb in these examples: it names an activity, even though it keeps the verb's ability to take an object. With a pronoun before a gerund, formal writing prefers the possessive: 'I dislike his coming late'; 'him coming late' is informal.
An infinitive phrase is to plus the base form of a verb, together with any object or adverbial: 'To master a language takes years' (subject); 'She wants to study abroad' (direct object); 'The aim is to improve' (subject complement). When the subject is long, English often moves it to the end and puts it in its place: 'It is wrong to tell lies', where it is a dummy subject and to tell lies is the real subject. The same test applies: if the phrase can be replaced by a noun such as this or something, it is working as a noun phrase.
An adjective may also head a noun phrase when it follows the and names a group of people or an abstract quality: the elderly, the unemployed, the unknown, the beautiful. These phrases behave like nouns. The elderly takes a plural verb because it denotes people: 'The elderly need support.' The unknown takes a singular verb when it refers to an abstract idea: 'The unknown frightens many people.' Not every adjective can be used this way; the pattern is learned with common examples such as the young, the old, the sick and the unemployed. Do not add a plural -s to the adjective.
A preposition is normally followed by a noun phrase, called its complement. The complement may be a noun phrase with a noun head: 'on the table'; a pronoun: 'with them'; or a gerund phrase: 'after finishing the work'. The preposition and its complement together form a prepositional phrase. That phrase may then do different work in the sentence: it may modify a noun ('the book on the desk') or act as an adverbial ('She studied in the room'). Keep the two levels apart: the noun phrase is the complement of the preposition; the prepositional phrase is the larger unit.
A verb phrase is built around a main verb, with or without auxiliary verbs: works; has worked; may have been working. In a sentence it normally functions as the predicate, the part that says what the subject does or is. In 'The students have been working hard', the verb phrase is have been working; hard is an adverbial, not part of the verb phrase. Do not confuse a verb phrase with a non-finite phrase: in 'To master a language takes years', to master a language is an infinitive phrase acting as the subject, not the predicate.
To identify the function of a bracketed expression, work in order. First find the finite verb of the sentence. Then ask who or what performs it for the subject, and who or what receives it for the object. After a linking verb such as be, seem, become, look or feel, the noun phrase that follows is a subject complement. After verbs such as call, name, elect or make, a noun phrase that describes the object is an object complement. If the expression follows a preposition, it is the complement of that preposition. Test a suspected noun phrase by replacing it with a pronoun: if it or them fits the same slot, the expression is doing noun work.
Common errors to avoid. Do not call every -ing word a verb: in 'Reading widely improves writing', reading widely is a gerund phrase subject, while writing is a noun object. Do not call an infinitive phrase a verb phrase when it is the subject. Do not treat the rich as singular. Do not call a prepositional phrase an adverb without checking what it modifies. Do not confuse an indirect object with an object complement: the indirect object receives, while the object complement describes. Keep the labels consistent with the grammar you have been taught, and name both the phrase type and its function when a question asks for the function.
The source's evaluation asks for the grammatical functions of expressions that were underlined, but underlining does not survive in a plain-text copy, so this lesson uses square brackets instead. The five items in practice Q6 are an equivalent exercise: four concern noun phrases and one a verb phrase. They are newly written and their answers are worked below; no answer is taken from the source's own evaluation. A written label is only the beginning of analysis: be ready to explain, in a full sentence, why the expression has the function you have named.

practice.question: Identify the head of each noun phrase and say whether the head is a noun, a pronoun or an adjective: (a) the two tall boys; (b) everyone in the hall; (c) those of us who stayed; (d) the elderly; (e) my best friend.
practice.answer: (a) boys, noun. (b) everyone, pronoun. (c) those, pronoun. (d) elderly, adjective. (e) friend, noun. The head is the word the modifiers depend on; a pronoun and an adjective-headed phrase can both fill the noun-phrase slot.

practice.question: Name the grammatical function of each bracketed noun phrase: (a) [The new bridge] was opened yesterday. (b) We visited [the old market]. (c) The teacher gave [the class] a test. (d) My sister is [a doctor]. (e) They called [the result] a surprise. (f) We waited at [the gate].
practice.answer: (a) subject. (b) direct object. (c) indirect object. (d) subject complement. (e) direct object. (f) complement of the preposition at. In (e), a surprise is the object complement that describes the result.

practice.question: Say whether each bracketed phrase is a gerund phrase or an infinitive phrase, and name its function: (a) [Swimming in the sea] is dangerous. (b) [To master a language] takes years. (c) She enjoys [reading novels]. (d) His hobby is [collecting stamps]. (e) He is good at [solving puzzles].
practice.answer: (a) gerund phrase, subject. (b) infinitive phrase, subject. (c) gerund phrase, direct object. (d) gerund phrase, subject complement. (e) gerund phrase, complement of the preposition at. Each phrase is a noun phrase because it fills a noun slot.

marking.criterion: (e) gerund phrase (1) and complement of the preposition (1)

practice.question: Answer on the adjective-headed noun phrases. (a) In 'The unemployed should receive training', identify the phrase and say what it denotes. (b) In 'The elderly need care', identify the head and explain the plural verb. (c) In 'The unknown can be frightening', identify the head and explain the singular verb. (d) Correct 'The unemployed is angry' and give the reason.
practice.answer: (a) the unemployed; the adjective unemployed is the head and denotes a group of people. (b) the elderly; elderly is an adjective head denoting elderly people as a group, so the verb need is plural. (c) the unknown; unknown is an adjective head denoting an abstract idea, so the singular can is used. (d) The unemployed are angry; the phrase denotes a group of people and takes a plural verb.

marking.criterion: (a) phrase identified and the group meaning
(d) are angry with the group reason

practice.question: For each sentence, write the prepositional phrase and its noun-phrase complement: (a) The keys are on the table. (b) She sat between the two boys. (c) He left after the meeting. (d) They spoke with great care. (e) The cat slept under the old car.
practice.answer: (a) on the table; the table. (b) between the two boys; the two boys. (c) after the meeting; the meeting. (d) with great care; great care. (e) under the old car; the old car. The whole prepositional phrase is the larger unit; the noun phrase is its complement.

marking.criterion: (a) on the table (1) and the table (1)
(b) between the two boys (1) and the two boys (1)
(c) after the meeting (1) and the meeting (1)
(d) with great care (1) and great care (1)
(e) under the old car (1) and the old car (1)

practice.question: Name the phrase type and the grammatical function of each bracketed expression: (a) [The committee] approved the plan. (b) They built [a new library]. (c) The headmaster is [a kind man]. (d) We waited at [the gate]. (e) The students [have been working] hard.
practice.answer: (a) noun phrase, subject. (b) noun phrase, direct object. (c) noun phrase, subject complement. (d) noun phrase, complement of the preposition at. (e) verb phrase, predicate. Four items concern noun phrases and one a verb phrase, matching the shape of the source evaluation without reusing its sentences.

marking.criterion: (d) noun phrase (1) and complement of the preposition (1)

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Agriculture vocabulary: general terms, livestock and fishery, with reviewed glosses
objectives: Define and use the sixteen general agriculture terms with reviewed glosses.
Distinguish closely related general terms such as arable land and arable farming, manure and fertilizer, and amortize and repay in full.
Define and use the ten livestock terms, including the corrected glosses for ranch and droppings.
Define and use the nine fishery terms, including the corrected glosses for cane pole and line, ripples and fishery.
Choose five taught words and use each in a complete, natural sentence.
Explain why the four flagged source glosses need correction and supply a corrected gloss for each.
lessons.body:
Agriculture is the practice of growing crops and raising animals for food, work and sale, and its vocabulary falls into three groups: general farming terms, livestock or animal husbandry, and fishery. This lesson teaches all three groups with a gloss, a class and an example sentence for each word. A gloss is useful only when it names the class of thing the word is — land, building, person, animal, meat, activity or business — and states the meaning in a full phrase. Several glosses in the source page need review: one describes farming instead of land, one is not intelligible as written, one has lost its verb, one headword is misspelt, and the fishery table has been flattened by the extraction so that one entry sits above its heading. This lesson reviews those points in original wording and does not edit the source.
Begin with the land and the farm buildings. An agrarian economy is one in which farming, rather than manufacturing or trade, provides most of the country’s income and employment. Land that is left fallow is not planted for a season or longer, so that the soil can recover; the adjective also appears in the phrase to lie fallow. An orchard is a piece of ground planted with fruit trees, and the word is not used for a field of vegetables. A seedling is a very young plant raised from a seed and ready to be moved into the field. A barn is a large farm building where grain, hay or other produce is stored, and it may also shelter animals. A nursery is a site where young plants are grown on for sale or for moving into the field; the same word also names a place where young children are cared for, so the context decides the sense.
The next group concerns what is grown and how the land is worked. Cash crops are grown to be sold rather than eaten by the farmer’s household; cotton, cocoa and groundnut are common examples, while maize grown for the family is a food crop. Arable land is land that can be ploughed and used for growing crops. The source gloss describes the activity of farming on such land, but the headword is the land itself, so the reviewed gloss above is the one to learn; arable farming is the activity of growing crops, as opposed to rearing animals. A mechanized farm is one on which machines do much of the work that would otherwise be done by hand or with animals. Manure is animal dung or other organic matter spread on the land to enrich the soil; it is a kind of fertilizer, though fertilizer is the wider term and includes manufactured products. A bumper harvest is a harvest that is larger than usual.
Five more general terms complete the list. A tendril is a thin, coiling stem or leaf part by which a climbing plant grips a support. Crop rotation is the practice of growing different crops in a planned order on the same land, so that the soil is not exhausted and pests are less likely to build up. An agricultural loan is money lent to a farmer, usually by a bank or a government scheme, to finance a farming project. Hybrid fruits are fruits produced by crossing two different varieties or species. Amortize means to pay off a debt gradually in regular instalments, each instalment covering part of the interest and part of the principal. The source gloss for amortize is not intelligible as written, so the reviewed gloss above should be used; the word belongs mostly to finance and accounting, and it can also mean to spread the cost of something over a period.
Livestock are the farm animals kept for food, work or other products: cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and poultry are the usual examples. A ranch is a large farm, especially in North America, where cattle, sheep or horses are raised. The source gloss has no verb and calls a ranch a confined space, but a ranch is normally extensive; a small enclosed area for animals is a pen or a paddock. Beef is meat from cattle. Droppings are the solid waste passed by animals or birds; the source headword is misspelt, and the correct spelling is droppings. A broiler is a young chicken raised for its meat. Dairy products are foods made from milk, such as butter, cheese and yoghurt. A pasture is grassland where grazing animals feed, and the verb is to pasture animals. A pullet is a young female chicken, especially one in its first laying season. To vaccinate an animal is to give it a vaccine, usually by injection, to protect it against disease, and the person trained to treat sick and injured animals is a veterinarian or veterinary doctor, informally a vet.
The fishery terms name the gear and the signs a fisher watches. A fish-net, also written fishing net, is a net made for catching fish. A cane pole and line is a simple fishing outfit: a long flexible cane with a line attached, used to reach fish in a pond, stream or shallow sea. The source gloss only says that the gear catches fish, which repeats the obvious and does not define it; the reviewed gloss above gives its make-up. Bait is food or a lure placed on a hook to attract fish, and an earthworm is a common natural bait. A float is a light object, often of cork or wood, fixed to the line so that it rests on the water and dips when a fish takes the bait; another name is a bobber. Ripples are the small rings and waves that spread across water when something disturbs its surface. The source ties ripples to a net or pole being thrown in, but the word itself names any small surface wave, and the reviewed gloss is the general one.
Four fishery terms name places and vessels. A trawler is a fishing boat that drags a large conical net, called a trawl, through the water behind it. A fish pond is an artificial pool of still water in which fish are reared. A fishery has two common senses: a stretch of sea or river where large numbers of fish are caught, and the industry of catching and selling fish. A business that breeds and rears fish for sale is more precisely a fish farm. The source presents these entries in a two-column table that the extraction flattens into tab-separated lines, so the fish-net row appears before the fishery heading; this lesson restates the terms in prose and does not depend on the table layout. A fishery is also not the same as a fish farm: the first is chiefly a catching ground or an industry, while the second is a breeding and rearing business.
Learn each word with its grammar and its common partners. Arable and agrarian are adjectives, and arable describes land or the type of farming; mechanized and hybrid are adjectives, and bumper is an adjective used before harvest. Ranch, pasture, harvest and farm all have verb uses: to ranch cattle, to pasture sheep, to harvest maize, to farm the land. Common collocations are to raise livestock, to spread manure, to plant seedlings, to rotate crops, to cast a net, to take the bait, to pay off a loan and to vaccinate animals. Keep these pairs apart: arable land is the ground and arable farming is the work; manure is organic and fertilizer is the wider term; beef is the meat and cattle are the animals; a ranch is extensive and a pen or paddock is enclosed; a fishery catches or processes fish and a fish farm breeds them; a float rests on the line and a ripple is a movement of the water.
When a vocabulary question asks you to use words in sentences, work in four steps. First name the class of thing the word is, because that keeps the gloss accurate. Second write the meaning as a full phrase rather than a single synonym, since a synonym may have a different range. Third add one natural collocation or sentence, because the collocation shows that the word is being used and not merely recognised. Fourth check the reviewed corrections in this lesson: arable land is land and not the activity, amortize is to pay a debt in instalments, a ranch is a large farm and not a confined space, the headword is droppings and not droopings, a cane pole and line is a rod with a line attached, ripples are any small surface waves, and a fishery is a catching ground or an industry rather than a breeding business. For the choose-five task, choose words you can use precisely, write one complete sentence for each word, and keep the word’s class and sense. The model sentences in practice Q5 show the standard expected.

practice.question: Match each word to its gloss. Words: (1) agrarian economy, (2) fallow, (3) orchard, (4) seedling, (5) barn, (6) cash crops, (7) manure, (8) bumper harvest, (9) tendril, (10) crop rotation. Glosses: A a harvest larger than usual; B a large farm building used for storing produce; C an economy in which farming provides most income and employment; D a thin coiling part by which a climbing plant grips a support; E land left unplanted so that the soil can recover; F crops grown to be sold rather than eaten by the farmer’s household; G a piece of ground planted with fruit trees; H a very young plant raised from a seed; I animal dung or organic matter spread to enrich the soil; J growing different crops in a planned order on the same land.

marking.criterion: (1) C, farming provides most income and employment
(2) E, land left unplanted so that the soil can recover
(3) G, ground planted with fruit trees
(4) H, a very young plant raised from a seed
(5) B, a large farm building used for storing produce
(6) F, crops grown to be sold rather than eaten
(7) I, animal dung or organic matter spread to enrich the soil
(8) A, a harvest larger than usual
(9) D, a thin coiling part that grips a support
(10) J, growing different crops in a planned order

practice.question: Write the word or phrase from this lesson that fits each description: (1) land that can be ploughed and used for crops; (2) a farm on which machines do much of the work; (3) money lent to a farmer to finance a project; (4) to pay off a debt gradually in regular instalments; (5) fruits produced by crossing two different varieties or species; (6) a place where young plants are raised for sale or transplanting; (7) a young female chicken in its first laying season; (8) a person trained to treat sick and injured animals.
practice.answer: (1) arable land; (2) mechanized farm; (3) agricultural loan; (4) amortize; (5) hybrid fruits; (6) nursery; (7) pullet; (8) veterinarian or veterinary doctor (informally vet).

practice.question: Each source gloss below is faulty. Write a corrected gloss and give a one-line reason. (1) “arable land: farming done on a piece of land good for tilling or ploughing.” (2) “amortize: this is to pay money in borrowed in bit.” (3) “ranches: this a farm/confined space for rearing of animals.” (4) “animal droopings: dung or faeces of animals or birds.”
practice.answer: (1) Arable land is land that can be ploughed and used for growing crops; the source gloss describes the farming activity rather than the land, which is what the headword names. (2) Amortize means to pay off a debt gradually in regular instalments, each covering part of the interest and part of the principal; the source wording is not intelligible. (3) A ranch is a large farm, especially in North America, where cattle, sheep or horses are raised; the source sentence has no verb, and a ranch is normally extensive rather than a confined space. (4) Droppings are the solid waste passed by animals or birds; the source headword is misspelt and the correct spelling is droppings, though the phrase animal droppings may be used.

marking.criterion: (1) corrected gloss: land that can be ploughed and used for crops
(1) reason: the source describes the activity, not the land

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Commonly misspelt words: patterns, dictionary checks and a keyed dictation
objectives: Explain the main patterns behind common spelling errors: consonant doubling, unstressed vowels, silent letters and suffix changes.
Spell the reviewed word list correctly and give the reason for each tricky letter.
Form related words correctly, such as business from busy and pronunciation from pronounce.
Correct misspellings in a passage and justify each correction.
Identify the defects in the source spelling table and state the corrected headword for ‘philandrer’.
Write a dictated passage accurately, including the twelve target words.
lessons.body:
English spelling is not random: most of the words that pupils get wrong belong to a small number of patterns, and learning the pattern is more reliable than memorising a letter string. This lesson reviews the words in the Week 4 list and supplies the analysis that the source page announces but does not give. It also records the defects in the source table: six rows repeat the correct form in the misspelt column, so no error is actually shown; two words from the table appear again in the further list, and two words repeat inside that list; and the headword ‘philandrer’ is itself misspelt. The corrected spellings below are the ones to learn, and the reasons are given so that a new word of the same type can be spelt with confidence.
The first pattern is consonant doubling. A final consonant is doubled before a suffix when the word ends in a single consonant after a single stressed vowel: refer becomes referred and incur becomes incurred, because the stress falls on the last syllable; but visit becomes visited and open becomes opened, because the stress falls earlier. The same rule explains beginning and preferred. Doubling is also fixed in the spelling of some words: accommodation has a double c where the prefix ac- meets commod-, and a double m; business has a double s from busy + ness; colossal has a single l and a double s; necessary has a single c and a double s; and misspell has a double s because it is mis + spell. Learn these as whole words, because the doubling is part of their history rather than a live rule.
The second pattern is the vowel in an unstressed syllable, which English pronounces weakly and so spells unpredictably. Separate has a in the second syllable and ends in -ate; the common error seperate uses e. Necessary has e in the second syllable and -ary at the end. Clarity is formed from clear + -ity with a change of vowel, so the noun has a in the first syllable and -ity at the end. Diligent has i in both of its first two syllables, and enmity has no i after the n. Business comes from busy + ness, so the y changes to i; pronunciation is built on -nunciation, not on the ou of pronounce; and maintenance is the noun from maintain but does not keep the -ain before -ance. When the vowel is weak, check the related word or the dictionary rather than trusting the sound.
The third pattern is the silent or unexpected letter. Acquaint and acquaintance keep the c before q, which the error aquaint drops. Foreigner keeps the silent g and ends in -er, not -or. Grievous and mischievous have no i after the v: they are grief + ous and mischief + ous, although the words are often said as if an extra syllable were present. Sandwich ends in -wich, not -witch. Pneumonia and psychiatric begin with a silent p, and psyche does the same; indict has a silent c; stethoscope keeps the th and the sc; obstetrician keeps the obstetr-; and choreography begins with ch pronounced as k. These letters are not decorative: they show the word’s history and often appear in related forms.
The fourth pattern is the suffix, which can change the base word or choose between lookalike endings. The ending -ous is used in grievous and mischievous, -ious in flirtatious, and -uous in continuous and promiscuous; the difference is fixed by each word and must be learned. Lovable drops the e of love before -able, and duly drops the e of due before -ly. The ending -cede appears in precede and accede, but the common verbs proceed, exceed and succeed use -ceed, and supersede uses -sede; there is no general rule beyond this small set. The noun pronunciation does not keep the ou of the verb pronounce, and the noun maintenance does not keep the ai of maintain. Check the suffix with the whole word family, not with the sound alone.
Some words in the list are simply unusual, often because they came into English from another language. Bibliography begins with biblio-, from the Greek word for book. Covenant has cov- at the start, not conv-. Expatiate has no n after the x. Herculean keeps the e after l; workaholic keeps the a before holic; limousine has limou-; buoy and buoyant keep the u before the oy; boulevard begins with bou-; hippopotamus has a double p and a single t; commission has a double m and a double s; surveillance has a double l; harassment has one r and a double s; embarrassment has a double r and a double s; agrarian has a in the second syllable; gubernatorial keeps the u after g and ends in -orial; onomatopoeia ends in -oeia; Ghanaian is Ghana + ian; burlesque ends in -esque; diarrhoea, in British spelling, has a double r followed by -hoea; and sarcasm ends in -asm. These are dictionary words: when a word looks foreign, look it up instead of sounding it out.
Three corrections to the source list need recording. First, the table’s misspelt column repeats the correct spelling for excitement, foreigner, misspell, necessary, receive and separate, so those six rows show no error; the common errors to avoid are excitment, foreignor, mispell, neccessary, recieve and seperate, and the lesson above gives the reason for each. Second, accommodation and maintenance appear both in the table and in the further list, and obstetrician and stethoscope appear twice in the further list; each word should be learned once. Third, the headword ‘philandrer’ is misspelt: the correct spelling is philanderer, formed from philander + -er, and the word means a man who has many casual love affairs. The source heading also promises an analysis of the words but gives none; the patterns in this lesson supply it.
Build a personal spelling list and check it properly. Write the word in a full sentence, not on its own, because the sentence shows the meaning and the grammar. Then write the related forms beside it: maintain, maintenance; pronounce, pronunciation; busy, business; grief, grievous; mischief, mischievous. Check the base form and the suffix separately, and check the syllable that carries the stress, since stress decides doubling. Use a dictionary that gives the British spelling and the syllable division, and note any variant, such as diarrhoea in British English and diarrhea in American English. Review the list by pattern rather than in one long column: group the doubling words, the weak-vowel words, the silent-letter words and the suffix words, and test yourself by writing the word from its meaning rather than by copying it.
The dictation in practice Q6 is the assessment for this lesson. The teacher reads the passage once at normal speed and then in short phrases, and the pupil writes it with correct spelling, capital letters and punctuation. The twelve target words are business, environment, clarity, maintenance, accommodation, diligent, continuous, pneumonia, separate, sandwich, grievous and necessary, and each correct spelling earns one mark; the marking guide in Q6 gives the passage and the target list. A dictation tests spelling in use, so a word that is correct in isolation but wrong in the sentence does not earn the mark. Before the dictation, revise the patterns above and the corrections in paragraph 7; after it, copy any wrong word into the personal list under its pattern.

practice.question: Correct the spelling of each word: (1) bussiness, (2) deligent, (3) enimity, (4) grevious, (5) pasttime, (6) pronouncaition, (7) sandwitch, (8) recieve, (9) foreignor, (10) excitment.
practice.answer: (1) business; (2) diligent; (3) enmity; (4) grievous; (5) pastime; (6) pronunciation; (7) sandwich; (8) receive; (9) foreigner; (10) excitement.

practice.question: For each word, name the letter or letter group that is most often got wrong, and give the reason: (1) accommodation, (2) business, (3) pronunciation, (4) maintenance, (5) mischievous, (6) grievous, (7) necessary, (8) separate, (9) environment, (10) acquaintance.
practice.answer: (1) the cc and mm: the prefix ac- joins commod-, which already has a double m. (2) the i: it comes from busy + ness, where y changes to i. (3) the nunci: the noun is built on -nunciation, not on the ou of pronounce. (4) the -tenance: the noun does not keep the -ain of maintain. (5) the o after v: mischief + ous, with no i before the o. (6) the o after v: grief + ous, with no i before the o. (7) the single c and double s: necessary has one c and ss. (8) the a in -par-: separate is spelt with a, not e. (9) the n before m: environ + ment places n before m. (10) the c after ac-: acquaint keeps the c before q.

marking.criterion: (1) cc and mm, with the ac- + commod- reason
(2) i, with the busy + ness reason
(5) o after v, with the mischief + ous reason
(6) o after v, with the grief + ous reason

practice.question: Rewrite this passage with all ten misspellings corrected: “Last term our class wrote a report on the enviroment. The teacher said that a good report needs clarity and a seperate list of sources. We checked every word in a dictionary and corrected our mispelling. The maintainance of the school garden was our topic, and we described the accomodation for the tools. A diligant pupil keeps a continious record of the work. It is neccessary to check the pronounciation of difficult words, and a mischievious mistake can spoil a good page.”
practice.answer: Corrected passage: “Last term our class wrote a report on the environment. The teacher said that a good report needs clarity and a separate list of sources. We checked every word in a dictionary and corrected our misspelling. The maintenance of the school garden was our topic, and we described the accommodation for the tools. A diligent pupil keeps a continuous record of the work. It is necessary to check the pronunciation of difficult words, and a mischievous mistake can spoil a good page.”

practice.question: Dictation. The teacher reads the following passage twice: first at normal speed, then in short phrases. Write it with correct spelling, capital letters and punctuation. “Last Friday our business club visited a farm outside the town. The environment was peaceful, and the farmer spoke with clarity about his work. He explained the maintenance of the barn and the accommodation for the workers. He said that a diligent farmer keeps a continuous record of feed and checks the animals for pneumonia every season. A separate shed holds the tools. At noon we ate a sandwich beside the orchard. We learned that a grievous spelling error can spoil a good report, so we practised the words necessary for our project.”
practice.answer: The passage for dictation is the text quoted in the question. Target words and their correct spellings: business, environment, clarity, maintenance, accommodation, diligent, continuous, pneumonia, separate, sandwich, grievous, necessary. Award one mark for each of the twelve target words spelt correctly in the pupil’s copy; do not deduct for other words, and do not award a mark for a target word that is omitted or used in the wrong place.
