lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Revision: word meaning in context with a keyed nearest-meaning set
objectives: Explain what ‘nearest in meaning’ requires and why exact synonyms are rare.
Identify the main context-clue types: definition, restatement, contrast, cause/effect, example and general knowledge.
Apply a step-by-step elimination method to nearest-meaning items.
Distinguish near-synonyms by connotation, strength and register.
Check a replacement for grammar, collocation and register.
Answer a keyed nearest-meaning set and explain both the choice and the rejection.
lessons.body:
This lesson is a revision set on word meaning in context. The Week 4 source ends with five multiple-choice items that ask for the word nearest in meaning to an underlined word, but the delivered text cannot be used as it stands: the underlining does not survive extraction, so the target word is invisible; the instruction says the options are lettered A to D although each item offers five; there is no answer key; and one target word is misspelt. The source options are therefore not used to infer a key. Instead, this lesson teaches the skill directly and supplies a new five-item set in the same format, with square brackets marking the target word and a worked answer for every item.
‘Nearest in meaning’ does not mean ‘identical in meaning’. Very few words are exact synonyms; most share a core sense but differ in strength, tone, grammar or the company they keep. A good answer is the option that can replace the target in that sentence without changing the sentence’s meaning or its tone. An option that is only loosely related, or that is stronger, weaker, more formal, more informal or more negative than the target, is not the nearest meaning even if it belongs to the same general area. Read the whole sentence first, because the context decides which sense of the target is active.
Context clues are the evidence the sentence gives you. A definition may follow the word, often after a dash, a colon or the phrase that is. A restatement may repeat the idea in different words. A contrast may be signalled by unlike, but, although or on the other hand. A cause or effect may be shown by so … that, because, therefore or as a result. An example may be introduced by such as, for example or including. General knowledge may also help, as when a sentence says that a thing broke when it fell, which tells you it was fragile. Name the clue before you look at the options; the clue narrows the meaning and stops the options from leading you.
Work through a nearest-meaning item in five steps. First read the sentence and cover the options. Second, predict a word or phrase of your own that would fit the target. Third, read the options and eliminate any that do not fit the sentence’s grammar: a noun cannot replace an adjective, and a countable form cannot replace an uncountable one. Fourth, eliminate options that are too broad, too narrow, opposite in meaning, or wrong in tone. Fifth, substitute the remaining option into the sentence and read it again; if the sentence still says the same thing in the same tone, you have the nearest meaning. If two options survive, choose the one that is closer in strength and register, not the one that is more familiar.
The commonest trap is a near-synonym with the wrong connotation. Childlike and childish both describe behaviour, but childlike is approving and childish is critical; thrifty and stingy both describe care with money, but thrifty is approving and stingy is not; famous and notorious both describe being widely known, but notorious adds disapproval. Other traps differ in strength: warm is weaker than hot, and surprised is weaker than astonished. A thesaurus lists words with similar cores; it does not tell you which one fits the sentence’s attitude. When an option feels stronger or more negative than the target, check whether the sentence supports that strength or attitude. If it does not, the option is a trap.
Grammar and register are part of meaning. A replacement must have the same part of speech and the same grammatical behaviour: refuse and deny are both verbs, but you refuse an invitation and you deny an accusation, so they are not interchangeable in every sentence. Evidence is uncountable, so proofs changes the grammar. Register matters too: commence is more formal than start, and kids is more informal than children; a replacement that changes the formality of the sentence is not the nearest meaning for a formal report. Collocation matters as well: we make a decision, not do a decision, and we take a risk, not make a risk. Learn the word with its grammar and its partners, not as a single synonym.
An answer key is useful only when it explains the choice. For each item, state the answer, give the context clue that supports it, and say why the tempting option is wrong. A full explanation has three parts: the target’s meaning in this sentence, the clue, and the reason for rejecting the nearest distractor. This is also how you should review your own work: if you chose an option but cannot name the clue, you guessed; if you can name the clue and the reason, you have learned the word. The practice items below use this three-part answer, and the marking gives credit for the explanation as well as the choice.
The source task needs correction before it can be used. The target words were underlined, and underlining is lost in a plain-text copy, so this lesson uses square brackets instead. The instruction says the options are lettered A to D, but every item has five options a to e; the lesson states the number of options in each item rather than repeating the mismatch. One target word is misspelt, and no key is supplied. The five source items also test the Week 2 skill of word meaning in context rather than any of the five Week 4 scheme objectives, so this set is labelled as revision of that skill and does not claim to assess the Week 4 topics. No answer is inferred from the source’s options.
Revise in three rounds. In the first round, learn the clue types and practise naming the clue in a sentence. In the second round, practise elimination: for each item, write down why each wrong option is wrong, not only why the right one is right. In the third round, write your own sentences for the words you missed and check them with a dictionary that gives the word’s grammar and collocations. Keep a list of near-synonym pairs that differ in tone (childlike/childish, thrifty/stingy, famous/notorious) and review them together, because the difference is easier to see side by side. The five-item practice set and its key are the model for the examination format.

practice.question: Each item has four options, A to D. Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in square brackets. (1) The committee’s report was [candid] about the school’s weaknesses. A secretive B frank C rude D lengthy. (2) The new rule was [beneficial] to both staff and pupils. A harmful B helpful C compulsory D popular. (3) Her explanation was so [concise] that everyone understood it at once. A brief B confusing C detailed D quiet. (4) The two accounts of the event were [consistent]. A conflicting B similar C exciting D doubtful. (5) The manager’s tone was [firm] but polite. A weak B decisive C angry D uncertain.
practice.answer: (1) B frank: candid means honest and direct, and frank is the closest; secretive is the opposite, rude adds offence, and lengthy is unrelated. (2) B helpful: beneficial means producing a good effect, and helpful is the closest; harmful is the opposite, while compulsory and popular describe other things. (3) A brief: concise means brief but complete, and brief is the closest; confusing and quiet are unrelated, and detailed is the opposite. (4) B similar: consistent here means agreeing with each other, and similar is the closest; conflicting is the opposite, while exciting and doubtful are unrelated. (5) B decisive: firm means determined and not easily changed, and decisive is the closest; weak and uncertain are the opposite, and angry is not implied.

marking.criterion: (1) explanation names the meaning and rejects a distractor
(2) explanation names the meaning and rejects a distractor
(3) explanation names the meaning and rejects a distractor
(4) explanation names the meaning and rejects a distractor
(5) explanation names the meaning and rejects a distractor

practice.question: Name the type of context clue that helps with the bracketed word, and quote the words that give the clue. Types: definition, restatement, contrast, cause/effect, example, general knowledge. (1) A [nomad], that is, a person who moves from place to place, carries a tent. (2) The teacher was [impartial]: she treated every pupil equally. (3) Unlike his [extravagant] brother, Musa saves most of his allowance. (4) The drought was so [severe] that the river dried up. (5) Citrus fruits such as oranges and lemons are rich in vitamin C.
practice.answer: (1) definition; clue ‘that is, a person who moves from place to place’. (2) restatement; clue ‘she treated every pupil equally’ after the colon. (3) contrast; clue ‘Unlike his … brother’ and ‘saves most of his allowance’. (4) cause/effect; clue ‘so … that the river dried up’. (5) example; clue ‘such as oranges and lemons’.

practice.question: In each item, one option is a near-synonym trap. Say which option is the trap and why it is not the nearest meaning. (1) The teacher praised the pupil’s [childlike] curiosity. A innocent B childish C young D small. (2) The scientist became [famous] for her discovery. A well-known B notorious C ordinary D secret. (3) He was [thrifty] with his money. A economical B stingy C poor D rich. (4) The room was [cozy]. A comfortable B cramped C cold D large. (5) Her reply was [frank]. A honest B rude C silent D long.
practice.answer: (1) B childish: it is critical, while childlike is approving. (2) B notorious: it adds disapproval, while famous is neutral. (3) B stingy: it is critical, while thrifty is approving. (4) B cramped: it is negative and suggests too little space, while cozy is warm and comfortable. (5) B rude: it adds offence, while frank is direct without being offensive.

marking.criterion: (4) reason: negative and suggests too little space

practice.question: A pupil replaced the bracketed word with the word after the arrow. Say whether the replacement is acceptable and why. (1) The committee will [commence] the meeting at noon. → start. (2) The [evidence] was conclusive. → proofs. (3) She [refused] the invitation. → denied. (4) The [rapid] growth surprised everyone. → quick. (5) He [implied] that he was unhappy. → inferred.
practice.answer: (1) Acceptable: start is the ordinary equivalent of commence, though less formal. (2) Not acceptable: evidence is uncountable, but proofs is countable, so the grammar changes. (3) Not acceptable: you refuse an invitation but deny an accusation or a fact, so the collocation and meaning change. (4) Acceptable: quick and rapid are both adjectives meaning fast, and quick growth is natural. (5) Not acceptable: the speaker implies and the listener infers, so the direction is reversed.

marking.criterion: (3) reason: refuse an invitation versus deny an accusation

practice.question: Use each word in a sentence that shows its meaning: (1) candid, (2) concise, (3) frugal, (4) impartial.
practice.answer: Model answers: (1) The head teacher was candid about the delay and explained what had gone wrong. (2) Her concise summary covered the main points in three sentences. (3) The frugal family saved money by repairing their clothes instead of replacing them. (4) A referee must be impartial and treat both teams alike. Any sentence that uses the word in its correct sense and reads naturally earns the marks.

marking.criterion: (1) candid used in its correct sense
(2) concise used in its correct sense
(3) frugal used in its correct sense
(4) impartial used in its correct sense

practice.question: Replace each bracketed word with a more precise word from this list: beneficial, enthusiastic, revised, straightforward, substantial, unanimous. The [good] effect of the new timetable was felt by every class. The committee made a [big] change to the lunch rules, and the [new] arrangement was [easy] to explain. Staff and pupils were [happy] with the result, so the vote was [together].
practice.answer: (1) good → beneficial: it states that the effect was helpful. (2) big → substantial: it states that the change was large in size or importance. (3) new → revised: it states that the arrangement was changed and updated. (4) easy → straightforward: it states that the arrangement was simple to explain. (5) happy → enthusiastic: it states strong approval or interest. (6) together → unanimous: it states that everyone agreed.

marking.criterion: (3) reason: states a changed, updated arrangement
(5) reason: states strong approval or interest

lessons.title: Kinds of sentences: clause counting, the five-way label and a keyed write-five task
objectives: Define a sentence in a way that covers statements, questions, commands and exclamations.
Identify finite clauses and count them rather than counting verbs.
Recognise and write simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences.
Explain the ‘multiple sentence’ label used by some course books and decide when to apply it.
Apply a five-step clause-counting method and check punctuation.
Write five sentences of different kinds with accurate clause counts and labels.
lessons.body:
A sentence is the smallest unit of writing that makes a complete statement, asks a complete question, gives a complete command or expresses a complete exclamation. Most sentences contain a finite verb and a subject, but the subject is not always written. A command such as ‘Close the door’ has an understood you as its subject, and an exclamation such as ‘How kind of you!’ expresses a complete reaction without a stated subject and verb. A definition that demands a written subject and verb therefore leaves out commands and exclamations, and a definition carrying a mistyped verb form cannot be relied on. Use the fuller definition: a sentence is a unit of complete sense built on at least one finite clause or, for commands and exclamations, on a recognised verbless pattern.
A clause is the unit to count. A finite clause contains a finite verb and normally its own subject. Coordination can join several verbs to one subject, and those verbs then form one clause with a compound predicate: in ‘Ada swept the floor, dusted the shelves and mopped the step’, there is one subject and one clause, however many actions are listed. A non-finite phrase is not a clause for this purpose: ‘To finish the work early, the team divided the tasks’ contains one finite clause, and the opening infinitive phrase is only an adverbial. Count subjects with their finite verbs, not the verbs on their own.
A simple sentence has exactly one main clause and no subordinate clause. It may be very short: ‘The gate opened.’ It may be long, because a single clause can carry many modifiers: ‘After a long delay caused by heavy rain, the weary travellers finally reached the small station on the hill.’ That sentence has one subject, the travellers, and one finite verb, reached. A compound subject does not add a clause: ‘Ada and Bola sang’ names two people but contains one clause. When you classify, cover the modifiers and find the finite verb first; if there is only one, and nothing is subordinated to it, the sentence is simple.
A compound sentence has two or more main clauses joined by coordination. The common coordinating conjunctions are and, but, or, nor, for, so and yet; a semicolon can also join two main clauses without a conjunction. Each main clause must be able to stand alone. ‘The rain stopped, and the children ran outside’ has two clauses. ‘The rain stopped, but the ground stayed wet’ has two. ‘You may wait here, or you may come back at four’ also has two, and this is the ‘or’ pattern that many textbook treatments name without illustrating. Do not join two main clauses with a comma alone: ‘The rain stopped, the children ran outside’ is a comma splice. Use a full stop, a semicolon or a conjunction.
Some course books add a fifth label, the multiple sentence, for three or more coordinated main clauses. The label describes a longer compound sentence; it does not describe a different grammatical structure. ‘The bell rang, the pupils lined up, and the teacher opened the door’ contains three main clauses: the bell rang; the pupils lined up; the teacher opened the door. If your class uses the five-way list, call this a multiple sentence and show the three clauses. If your class uses the four standard kinds, call it a compound sentence and still show the three clauses. Never use the label to inflate a sentence that has one subject and several verbs: ‘The bell rang, echoed down the corridor and woke the caretaker’ has one clause, because the bell is the subject of all three verbs. Whether the five-way list is used in this course is a decision for the teacher; the clause count is the same either way.
A complex sentence consists of one main clause plus at least one subordinate clause. One subordinate clause is enough to make the sentence complex, and two or more subordinate clauses do not make it compound, because there is still only one main clause. Subordinate clauses are introduced by subordinators such as because, although, when, while, if, unless, since, after, before and so that, or by relative words such as who, which, whose, that and where. The subordinate clause may come first: ‘When the rain stopped, we left the field.’ It may come second: ‘We left the field because the ground was soft.’ It may be a relative clause inside the main clause: ‘The girl who won the prize smiled.’ A complex sentence with two subordinate clauses remains complex: ‘Although it rained, we stayed because the hall was warm.’
A compound-complex sentence contains at least two main clauses together with one or more subordinate clauses. Build it by adding a subordinate clause to a compound sentence, or a second main clause to a complex sentence. ‘When the rain stopped, the match resumed, and the spectators cheered’ has one subordinate clause, when the rain stopped, and two main clauses, the match resumed and the spectators cheered. ‘The teacher who marked the scripts returned them, but two pupils were absent’ has the relative clause who marked the scripts inside the first main clause, a second main clause introduced by but, and therefore two main clauses in all. Count the main clauses first; if there are at least two, then look for a subordinate clause. Only then use this label.
Use the same counting method every time. Step one: find every finite verb and underline it. Step two: give each finite verb its subject. Step three: decide whether each clause can stand alone; if it can, it is a main clause, and if it depends on a subordinator or a relative word, it is subordinate. Step four: count. One main clause and no subordinate clause gives a simple sentence. At least two main clauses with no subordinate clause give a compound sentence. One main clause with at least one subordinate clause gives a complex sentence. Two or more main clauses with at least one subordinate clause give a compound-complex sentence. Step five: check the punctuation. A comma alone cannot carry two main clauses; a comma normally follows an opening subordinate clause; a relative clause is usually not set off by commas when it identifies the noun it modifies.
The commonest errors are counting mistakes. A sentence with a compound subject is not compound: ‘The captain and the coach agreed’ has one clause. A sentence with a compound predicate is not compound: ‘She packed her bag and left’ has one clause. A sentence with two verbs is not automatically compound, and a sentence with one subordinate clause is not automatically compound-complex. A comma splice is not a compound sentence, because punctuation alone does not make a clause coordinate. A relative clause after a comma may still be subordinate, as in ‘My brother, who lives in Lagos, is visiting’, which is complex, not compound. Commands have no written subject but are still sentences. Finally, do not call every long sentence complex: length is not the test, and clause count is.
The Week 5 source needs review before reuse, and this lesson records what was found without copying it. Its outline names three kinds, but the teaching that follows covers five, and the outline calls the last one by a slashed name. Its definition of a sentence contains a mistyped plural verb and leaves out commands. Its two multiple-sentence examples may each contain fewer than three main clauses, because one subject can carry several coordinated predicates. Its compound section names ‘or’ but illustrates only ‘and’ and ‘but’. Its complex definition uses a singular noun after ‘one or more’. Its single compound-complex example reuses the compound example with a clause added. This lesson supplies fresh examples, a clause-counted method and a keyed five-sentence task. It does not correct the source bytes and does not settle the five-way label for the course; that choice stays with the teacher, and either label is accepted when the clause count is shown.

practice.question: Answer briefly. (a) Give a definition of a sentence that covers commands and exclamations as well as statements. (b) Explain why ‘Sit down’ is a sentence although it has no written subject. (c) Identify the finite verb and its subject in each: (i) The workers repaired the roof before noon. (ii) Please close the gate. (iii) How cold the wind is! (iv) The pupils have finished their project. (v) There are three chairs in the hall.
practice.answer: (a) A sentence is a unit of complete sense built on at least one finite clause or, for commands and exclamations, on a recognised verbless pattern. (b) It is a complete command; the subject is the understood you, which is not written in the imperative. (c)(i) repaired, the workers. (ii) close, you (understood). (iii) is, the wind. (iv) have finished, the pupils. (v) are, three chairs (the existential there is not the subject).

marking.criterion: (a) complete-sense definition allowing commands and exclamations
(b) understood you named as the subject

practice.question: Classify each sentence as simple, compound, complex or compound-complex, and give the number of main and subordinate clauses. (a) The old bridge collapsed during the storm. (b) The hall was full, so the organisers opened the side door. (c) Because the bus was late, we missed the first lesson. (d) The pupil who won the debate thanked her teacher, and the audience applauded. (e) The rain fell, the wind rose, and the lights went out.
practice.answer: (a) simple: one main clause, no subordinate clause. (b) compound: two main clauses, no subordinate clause. (c) complex: one main clause, one subordinate clause. (d) compound-complex: two main clauses, one subordinate clause. (e) compound: three main clauses, no subordinate clause; this is the longer compound that some books call a multiple sentence.

practice.question: For each sentence, count the main and subordinate clauses and name the kind. (a) When the fire alarm rang, the pupils left the building quietly. (b) The cook prepared the meal and washed the plates. (c) My aunt, who lives in Kaduna, sent us a parcel, but it arrived late. (d) The team trained hard although the ground was muddy and the coach was ill.
practice.answer: (a) one main clause, one subordinate clause (when the fire alarm rang); complex. (b) one main clause, no subordinate clause; the two verbs share one subject, so this is a simple sentence with a compound predicate. (c) two main clauses, one subordinate clause (who lives in Kaduna); compound-complex. (d) one main clause, two subordinate clauses (although the ground was muddy; and the coach was ill); complex.

practice.question: Each pupil’s analysis is wrong. Name the error and give the correct classification. (a) ‘She packed her bag and left’ is compound because it has two verbs. (b) ‘The room was cold, we closed the windows’ is compound. (c) ‘Although it rained, we stayed because the hall was warm’ is compound-complex. (d) ‘The visitors arrived and the choir sang’ is complex because it uses a conjunction.
practice.answer: (a) One subject carries a compound predicate, so there is one clause; the sentence is simple. (b) Two main clauses are joined by a comma alone, which is a comma splice; it is not a correct compound sentence. Write ‘The room was cold, so we closed the windows’ for a compound sentence, or ‘Because the room was cold, we closed the windows’ for a complex one. (c) There is one main clause and two subordinate clauses, so the sentence is complex, not compound-complex. (d) And is a coordinating conjunction and both clauses can stand alone, so the sentence is compound, not complex.

marking.criterion: (b) comma splice named (1) and a correct rewrite or classification (1)
(c) one main clause with two subordinate clauses (1) and complex (1)
(d) and is coordinating with two main clauses (1) and compound (1)

practice.question: Combine each pair or group into the kind named. (a) The bell rang. The pupils went to their classes. → compound, using and. (b) The match was cancelled. The ground was waterlogged. → complex, using because. (c) The teacher entered. The class stood up. The monitor called for silence. → compound with three main clauses. (d) The train was delayed. We reached the station early. We still missed it. → compound-complex with one subordinate clause, using although. (e) The road was closed. We took the longer route. → complex with the subordinate clause first, using since.
practice.answer: Model answers: (a) The bell rang, and the pupils went to their classes. (b) The match was cancelled because the ground was waterlogged. (c) The teacher entered, the class stood up, and the monitor called for silence. (d) Although the train was delayed, we reached the station early, but we still missed it. (e) Since the road was closed, we took the longer route.

marking.criterion: (a) two main clauses joined by and with a comma
(b) one main clause with because + subordinate clause
(d) two main clauses and one subordinate clause
(e) subordinate clause first, comma, then main clause

practice.question: Write five sentences of your own, one for each requirement: (a) a simple sentence of at least twelve words; (b) a compound sentence with two main clauses joined by but; (c) a compound sentence with three main clauses (label it multiple if your class uses the five-way list); (d) a complex sentence with an opening subordinate clause; (e) a compound-complex sentence with two main clauses and one subordinate clause. After each sentence, write the number of main and subordinate clauses. Do not reuse the examples in this lesson.
practice.answer: Model answers. (a) After checking the locks twice, the caretaker walked slowly home through the empty streets. One main clause, no subordinate clause. (b) The library was closed, but the reading room stayed open until six. Two main clauses, no subordinate clause. (c) The generator failed, the backup light came on, and the nurse continued the lesson. Three main clauses, no subordinate clause; multiple if the five-way label is used. (d) Although the road was flooded, the bus reached the school on time. One main clause, one subordinate clause. (e) When the visitors arrived, the choir sang, and the head teacher welcomed them. Two main clauses, one subordinate clause. Any five sentences that meet the stated requirements and carry a correct clause count earn the marks.

marking.criterion: (a) simple, at least twelve words, 1 main and 0 subordinate
(b) compound with but, 2 main and 0 subordinate
(c) three main clauses with an accepted label
(d) complex with an opening subordinate clause

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Expository essay: features, a worked plan for ‘Honesty is the Best Legacy’ and a marked task
objectives: Define an expository essay and distinguish it from narrative and persuasive writing.
Identify the features of a strong expository essay.
Plan an expository essay with a thesis and three ordered body points.
Use a worked plan for ‘Honesty is the Best Legacy’.
Write an introduction and a body paragraph that explain rather than narrate.
Apply a marking scheme to an expository essay task.
lessons.body:
An expository essay explains. Its job is to make a subject clear to a reader who does not already understand it: what the thing is, how it works, why it matters, what kinds exist, or how a process is carried out. It may recommend, but explanation is its main work; it may describe, but description serves the explanation. It does not tell a story for its own sake, and it does not rely on emotional appeal. The writer’s presence is modest: the subject, not the writer’s feelings, holds the centre of the essay.
Five features distinguish a strong expository essay. First, a clear thesis: one sentence that states what the essay will explain. Second, a logical order: the points follow a plan such as cause to effect, problem to solution, general to particular, or step by step. Third, paragraph unity: each paragraph makes one point, announced in a topic sentence. Fourth, explanation before illustration: the writer explains the point in general terms, then gives an example, and then shows how the example supports the point. Fifth, an objective register: formal vocabulary, complete sentences, few contractions, and a conclusion that closes the explanation rather than opening a new topic.
Plan before you write. Read the question and underline its key terms; define them in the introduction. Brainstorm on rough paper, then group the ideas into three body points. Choose an order that a reader can follow. Write a one-sentence thesis that names the three points. Draft an outline with a topic sentence for each body paragraph and one example or piece of evidence under each. Check that every note serves the thesis and delete the rest. An outline is a promise to the reader: the essay must keep it.
Here is a worked plan for ‘Honesty is the Best Legacy’. Define honesty as truthfulness and fair dealing, and a legacy as what one generation passes to the next. Thesis: honesty is the best legacy because it builds trust, protects a good name and teaches the young by example. Body one, trust: explain that trust lowers the cost of every relationship, because people do not have to check, guard or bargain at every step; illustration, a pupil who returns a lost wallet is trusted with responsibility. Body two, reputation: explain that deceit creates a hidden debt that must be paid later; illustration, a candidate who cheats may gain one grade but loses the reference that opens a career. Body three, teaching by example: explain that children learn conduct by watching adults; illustration, a trader whose weights are always exact keeps customers for decades. Conclusion: restate the thesis, say that the real inheritance is character rather than money, and recommend that families and schools reward truthfulness.
Model introduction. ‘Every family hopes to leave something behind: land, savings, a house, a name. Yet the most valuable thing a parent can pass on cannot be counted at the bank. Honesty, the habit of telling the truth and dealing fairly even when a lie would be easier, is the best legacy because it builds trust, protects a good name and teaches the young by example. This essay explains why these three gifts outlast any material inheritance.’
Model body paragraph on trust. ‘Honesty builds trust, and trust makes every relationship cheaper to maintain. When people expect the truth, they do not need to verify every receipt, monitor every promise or repeat every instruction. A pupil who finds a wallet in the classroom and returns it unopened receives something more useful than thanks: the teacher knows that the pupil can be trusted with the class register, the keys or the money for a trip. The same principle operates in a workplace, where a worker who reports a mistake early is given more responsibility than one who hides it. Trust, once earned, becomes a form of capital that a family can draw on for years.’
Model body paragraph on example. ‘Honesty is also a legacy because it is taught by example rather than by instruction. Children learn what adults do far more reliably than what adults say, so a parent who returns extra change to a shopkeeper is giving a lesson that no lecture can replace. A trader who keeps honest scales may lose a little in the short term, but customers who value fair dealing return for decades and bring their friends. In this way an honest reputation passes from parent to child and from one generation of customers to the next, long after the original trader has left the market.’
Model conclusion. ‘Honesty, then, is the best legacy for three reasons: it creates trust, it protects a name that deceit would destroy, and it teaches the next generation by example. Money can be spent, land can be sold and houses can fall into disrepair, but a reputation for integrity continues to work for the family that inherits it. Parents and schools should therefore reward truthfulness openly, forgive honest mistakes and refuse to treat a clever lie as a success. The greatest gift is not what a family owns but what it is known for.’
The commonest failure is turning exposition into narrative. A story can appear only as a brief example inside a paragraph that explains a general point; it must not become the spine of the essay. In the friendship-saying outline, the incident is evidence for an explanation of loyalty, not the plot of the essay. Other faults: a thesis that merely repeats the title; points that are listed but never explained; paragraphs that begin with an example and never state the point; slang and contractions in a formal task; a conclusion that adds a new argument; and length used as a substitute for thought. A newspaper article has its own conventions, such as a headline, short paragraphs and a named writer, but its explanatory purpose is unchanged.
The Week 5 source gives a one-sentence definition and two sample plans but no teaching of features, no model text, no length and no marks; its evaluation names a title only. Its sanitation plan is framed as a newspaper article and carries a stray label, while its friendship plan asks for an incident, which pulls towards narrative. The title task cannot be taught or marked from the source. This lesson supplies the features, a worked plan, model paragraphs, a marked task and a marking scheme. It does not copy the source’s plans or sentences, does not treat the 2nd Term essay-types lesson as coverage, and does not infer a marking scheme from the source.

practice.question: Name the main purpose of each extract (explain, persuade, narrate or describe), and say whether it could stand in an expository essay. (a) Rainwater harvesting collects roof run-off in tanks so that a household can store water for the dry season. (b) Vote for me, and I will repair every road in this ward by December. (c) The day I lost my fare, a stranger paid it, and I have never forgotten her kindness. (d) The market opens at dawn: first the vegetable sellers arrive, then the cloth traders, and by seven the lanes are full. (e) A balanced diet contains carbohydrates for energy, proteins for growth and repair, and vitamins and minerals for protection.
practice.answer: (a) explain; yes, because it defines and explains a process. (b) persuade; no, because it appeals for a vote rather than explaining. (c) narrate; no as the spine of the essay, though it could appear as a brief example. (d) describe; only if the description supports an explanation of how the market works. (e) explain; yes, because it classifies the parts of a balanced diet and their functions.

marking.criterion: (c) narrate and not acceptable as the spine
(d) describe and acceptable only in a supporting role

practice.question: Write a one-sentence thesis for each topic. Each thesis must name three points that the essay will explain. (a) The importance of school libraries. (b) Why refuse collection matters in a town. (c) How to revise for examinations. (d) The value of practical science lessons. (e) Why honesty matters in trading.
practice.answer: Model theses: (a) A school library matters because it gives pupils independent reading, a quiet place to study and support for research across subjects. (b) Regular refuse collection matters because it prevents disease, keeps public spaces usable and protects the town’s water supply. (c) Effective revision depends on a timetable, active recall and regular rest. (d) Practical science lessons are valuable because they develop observation, make theory concrete and teach safe handling of equipment. (e) Honesty matters in trading because it earns repeat customers, prevents disputes and builds a reputation that outlasts any single sale.

marking.criterion: (a) clear position plus three named points
(b) clear position plus three named points
(c) clear position plus three named points
(d) clear position plus three named points
(e) clear position plus three named points

practice.question: Arrange these notes into a five-paragraph plan for a newspaper article on improving sanitation in your area, and state the role of each paragraph. Notes: weekly collection should be scheduled and announced; dirty surroundings spread disease and lower morale; the council should repair the broken drain on Market Road; households should use covered bins and stop dumping in the stream; the community should organise a monthly clean-up; sanitation means the safe management of waste and dirty water.
practice.answer: Paragraph 1 (introduction): define sanitation as the safe management of waste and dirty water, and state that dirty surroundings spread disease and lower morale. Paragraph 2 (first body point): the council should repair the broken drain on Market Road, because standing water breeds mosquitoes. Paragraph 3 (second body point): households should use covered bins and stop dumping in the stream. Paragraph 4 (third body point): weekly collection should be scheduled and announced, and the community should organise a monthly clean-up. Paragraph 5 (conclusion): summarise the three measures and urge residents and the council to act together.

marking.criterion: paragraph 1 uses the definition and the problem
paragraph 2 places the drain repair as a council measure
paragraph 3 places covered bins and dumping as a household measure
paragraph 4 combines collection and the clean-up
paragraph 5 is a conclusion with no new measure

practice.question: For the ‘Honesty is the Best Legacy’ plan, write a topic sentence and one supporting example or piece of evidence for each of the three body paragraphs, and one closing sentence for the conclusion.
practice.answer: Model answers. Body one: ‘Honesty builds trust, which makes every relationship easier to manage.’ Example: a pupil who returns a lost wallet is trusted with the class register. Body two: ‘Honesty protects a good name, while deceit creates a debt that must be paid later.’ Example: a candidate who cheats may gain a grade but loses the reference that opens a career. Body three: ‘Honesty is taught by example, and children copy what adults do.’ Example: a trader with honest scales keeps customers for decades. Conclusion: ‘The real inheritance is character, not property.’

marking.criterion: body one topic sentence and a relevant example
body two topic sentence and a relevant example
body three topic sentence and a relevant example
closing sentence restates the thesis without a new point

practice.question: A pupil wrote this body paragraph: ‘Honesty is good. My uncle is honest. One day he found a phone and gave it back. Everybody should be honest because it is good.’ Name two faults and rewrite the paragraph so that it explains one point.
practice.answer: Faults: there is no topic sentence or explanation, so the paragraph asserts instead of explaining; the example is not connected to a general point, and the reasoning is circular (‘good because it is good’). Model rewrite: ‘Honesty earns trust because it shows that a person can be relied on when no one is watching. When the pupil’s uncle found a phone and returned it, the owner learned that lost property could be recovered and the family gained a reputation for fair dealing. Trust of this kind is valuable because it makes future dealings simpler and safer.’

marking.criterion: fault one named: no topic sentence or explanation
fault two named: an unconnected example or circular reasoning
rewrite has a topic sentence that states one point
rewrite explains and connects the example

practice.question: Write the introduction and first body paragraph (about 150 words in total) of an expository essay on ‘Honesty is the Best Legacy’. Use the worked plan, then list the three points your essay would develop.
practice.answer: Model answer. ‘Honesty is often treated as a rule for children, yet it is better understood as a form of wealth that a family passes down. A legacy is what one generation hands to the next, and honesty, meaning consistent truthfulness and fair dealing, is the most durable part of that inheritance because it creates trust, guards reputation and shapes conduct by example. The first gift is trust. People who deal with an honest family do not need to double-check every figure or repeat every agreement. When a shopkeeper returns the extra money that a customer has paid by mistake, the customer returns, brings friends and speaks well of the shop; the small sum given back is an investment in years of custom. Trust earned in ordinary transactions becomes the foundation on which larger opportunities are offered.’ The three points are trust, reputation and teaching by example.

marking.criterion: definition or context in the introduction
body paragraph has a topic sentence for the first point
explanation supported by a relevant example
links the example back to the point

evidence.explanation: The original row defines monophthongs as pure, single-element vowels (examples /e/ and /i/) against double-element diphthongs (/ei/, /iƏ/). The heading, the scheme row and the body spell the word differently ('Monophthongs' in the scheme, 'Monothongs' in the body); the body also writes the schwa symbol as /Ə/. This row is replaced in delivery by SUP-SS1-ENGLISH-PHONETICS-T1 (correction SS1-02-english-COR-005).

The replacement lists the twelve pure vowels and says a diphthong 'moves between vowel qualities', which implies the contrast, but it does not define a monophthong or say that a pure vowel is a single steady quality. The definition objective is therefore partly covered; the gap is tracked by open item ENGLISH-T1-W03-PHONETICS-REPLACEMENT-SCOPE and queue item ENG-LES-W03-MONOPHTHONGS-SCOPE.

The supplement defines a monophthong as a pure vowel whose quality stays steady, written with one symbol, and defines a diphthong as a glide between two vowel qualities within one syllable. It gives the twelve symbols and notes the eight diphthongs in British English. With the replacement's symbol list, the definition objective is now covered; the scope gap recorded by ENGLISH-T1-W03-PHONETICS-REPLACEMENT-SCOPE is closed. Authored 2026-11-03; content approval PENDING and verification DEFERRED.
